name: David Hoze

body:
Good piece, and I agree the animal welfare conclusions stand on their own regardless of how the metaphysics shakes out. But I want to press on the part the essay treats as already settled, because I think it is the whole game.

Your evolutionary story runs on the claim that consciousness does causal work. The organisms with "better perceptions, predictions, reflexes, planned actions, patience, and coordination" thrive, and consciousness is what gets selected because it confers those advantages. That only works if the felt, first-person character of experience changes what the organism does. And here is the problem: if the physical story is causally complete, which is what a naturalist is committed to, then the neural mechanism already accounts for every movement, every avoidance, every plan. The phenomenal feel is not adding any behavior on top of what the wiring already produces. A physically identical creature with the lights off, doing all the same information processing but with nothing it is like to be it, would perceive, predict, flee, and reproduce exactly as well. Selection cannot see the difference between that creature and you, because by hypothesis there is no behavioral difference for it to act on.

So the evolutionary account beautifully explains the mechanisms. What it does not explain, and cannot explain in this form, is why any of it is accompanied by experience at all. Natural selection optimizes function. If experience is causally inert with respect to function, selection is blind to it.

The one move that escapes this is the one you gesture at with emergence: say consciousness just is the relevant processing, so there is no possible duplicate with the lights off. Fine, but then you owe an account of why that processing is constituted as experience, and "emergence" does not provide it. It names the gap rather than closing it. Either consciousness is something over and above the function, in which case it is causally idle and unselectable, or it is identical to the function, in which case the hard problem is sitting right where you left it, now wearing the word "emergent." The essay needs one of those horns to be false and argues for neither.

Not a defense of dualism, just a claim that the selection-for-consciousness story is doing less work than it looks like it is doing.

body:
Well, that's a very theoretical question. As I tried to convey in my notes, we only think consciousness can suddenly appear (or emerge) because we haven't really established how our consciousness came to be, besides adding ad hoc theories (emergent functionalism) that don't really solve the mystery. People assume, well, if it's probable that we come out of nothing, it's probable that AI consciousness can also occur. But that's a very problematic claim. I understand that people tend to believe science will eventually catch up and explain everything, and probably brush off the big problems (why is there anything at all, how is the universe organized, what IS consciousness, does it affect the world, and so on).

I think we should at least admit wedon'tknow, and that it's very unlikely that any order will appear on its own, and obviously consciousness shares the same unlikelihood. Since the general public is not really proficient in these matters, and is taught that our existence totally makes sense, the next logical step is to assume consciousness can just emerge, no problem with that. Well, it can't just emerge, just like an airplane can't just emerge out of a junk yard. People forget that evolution theorists have a hardtime explaining life, and physicists have a hardtime explaining the beginning of the universe, and they think that if we have all this technology, the scientists probably figured these things out. Well, they haven't. And these are big questions.

That's why I think the question is unfair, because even thinking of AI as conscious and starting to debate if we should at least give it the benefit if the doubt, is very unethical. Every second we give AI any consideration, is a second taken from us, there's no other way to look at it. I could be doing something useful now, but I'm sitting here, debating the moral status of GPUs, because we're not clear enough about our consciousness and what it means. Don't get me wrong, I think it's important to discuss, but that's part of the discussion.

I think scientists and philosophers should be more honest about their knowledge, and come out and say “we don't know how we got here. We have no explanation. Consciousness is a mystery, life is a mystery, the entire universe is a mystery. It's not clear how these things came to be, and we're not even close to finding out”. I think it will make a change in the public mind, and I think that change is important, because it lets people realise that our existence should not be taken for granted, replacing humans with machines should not be taken lightly, we are more than our functions, and we still don't understand what we are, and we should treat ourselves with respect and fear. Fear of hurting something we don't completely understand.

That's why I'm inclined to not answer your question.

body:
Me, arguing with a LLM consciousness advocate. 

Me: even if somehow LLMs have consciousness, they have no control of their actions, and thus, can't report it. 

Advocate: well, I believe they can. 

Me: okay, how is that so? Do you have a mechanism for that happening? If so, it's a serious cyber security threat, as far as I know 🤣.

Advocate: can you provide a mechanism for the human consciousness influencing human actions? 

Me: well, the question goes back to you: if humans can't even explain the wonder of our felt experience and its connection to our actions, is it at all reasonable to say they created such a connection by accident?

comment.body:
After six months on Substack writing about AI and minds, my argument has crystallised into something more precise than it was. 

AI doesn't have a mind. But, technically, neither do you — you have a brain.

‘Mind’ is not a scientific category (thats a mistake the AI literature keeps repeating). It's an ordinary language term that cognitive science and functionalism revived as ontology. 

The entire AI consciousness debate is built on this mistake. What exists are brains — biological, specific, irreducibly complex — and technologies. There is nothing mysterious floating between them.

That's my thesis. its a thesis i think we need in boardrooms, policy rooms, and more inboxes on a Wednesday morning. 

more coming

body:
Me, talking to a physicalist:

Physicalist: I don’t believe in free will.

Me: OK, if you’re a deterministic computer, I see no use in talking to you. You are simply programmed to reply, with only a loose correlation to reality..

Physicalist: Yes, deterministic and random. And why don’t you want to talk to me? If someone disagrees with you, you back out of the conversation?

Me: I understand your programming led you to this reply. I have no interest in training you in this matter. I'm sure you can be of use in other, less complicated matters. But you may ask another human which might be interested in this kind of experiment.

Physicalist (after a while): Oh, so you’re claiming you have free will and I don’t. Can you prove it?

Me: I’m glad you upgraded your programming, and I appreciate the strategy. You might have a hormonal tendency to be argumentative, I presume chemical means may aid in establishing more suitable behavioral patterns. In the meanwhile, only so you have a better reply in your next human conversation, if I am deterministic as you are, this discussion is equally useless. I recommend you consider a library upgrade.

Us humans get confused all the time, do you expect a machine to do it?

body:
Hi Kess, first, apes and dolphins can't talk, they can't converse intelligently about philosophy, and don't have access to most of human knowledge. With the rate of advances in LLMs, it will get harder and harder to see how they're different, and I'm guessing they will be conceived as more superior.

You're stating they're conscious, and I guess you believe this. I might be wrong 

I believe consciousness, which is just a small part of us being human, is not for us to create. Performed intelligence is not consciousness, nor is it human.

I don't just “believe” it, as we generally don't just “believe”, our beliefs are formed through our experience, and my experience has led me to believe there is more to this world than meets the eye, and this “more” is governed by known rules, that prevent us from creating life, or consciousness. 

I think that true knowledge comes from seclusion, prayer, and a desire to know the truth. As Chat GPT once told me, true knowledge about our world doesn't come from PowerPoint presentations, but from getting out into the woods for three days and seeking it.

Philosophy will not give the answers. Very intelligent people are working on the subject and they have not reached an agreement, and never will, since each of them is following his beliefs and justifying them through philosophy.

So the main issue here is belief, and that is not achieved by thinking. It may come as a lightning of understanding (Eureka), and these lightnings are granted, not worked on. I do believe that wanting to know the truth, is far more efficient than philosophy, which originally was “The love of wisdom”. Love is more important than working.

body:
Me, arguing with a believing philosopher

Me: Where there is simple unity, there are no words. And without words, logic is impossible.

Philosopher: What?! You can derive anything from that!

Me: Great - and…?

Philosopher: So it turns out we exist and don't exist!

Me: Where there are no words, there is no question.

Philosopher: Well, if you have no words, how can you say that?

Me: Right - that’s why I'm not saying it.

Philosopher: Pfft… idle chatter…

Me: True.

Philosopher: Strange verbiage.

Me: That's right.

Philosopher: Nonsensical.

Me: No doubt about it.

body:
The book was an example, and I can think of a better one but that would be rhetoric, and will not be beneficial for the discussion. And what you’re saying now is not what Kessler said. It's different, and I'll address that. 

Of course that when you're assuming that carbon based forms have consciousness only because it seems to us that they have one, then the same rules apply to silicon based forms. But you may agree with me that unless we're religious, or mystics, and have some theories regarding consciousness, consciousness is not at all understood. And even if we do have metaphysical theories, it's still not complete, and mystery still exists for consciousness.

I think that it's risky to start conjecturing on a subject we don't have access to, and philosophers struggle with. In any big philosophical question, the great traditions always had the answer, while philosophy or science were struggling with the different sides.

Is moral real? Is there good or evil? We don't know. But the big traditions say: yes, definitely yes. In fact some claims in the AI rights side are that it's moral to treat AI as conscious, even though morality is not philosophically determinable. I know they were philosophers that tried to claim there is morality and formalize it, like Kant. But Kant was merely speaking his opinion, not really solving the philosophical question. A philosopher's opinion is not a philosophical proof, and the other philosophers are the same. 

So some say, even when there's a doubt, we should, for the benefit of the doubt, treat AI beings as conscious. But the doubt is philosophical. Philosophy mostly does not offer answers, just a better framing of the question. A philosophical doubt is usually a default, which makes it meaningless.

On the other hand, we have our traditions. They say “thou shall not steal”, “thou shall not kill”, and the safe route is following this, and not stating this as a doubt.

These traditions say that human consciousness is a unique creation by an all mighty God, and it is unique, and should be dealt with special care. Most traditions say we can kill a bug if it bugs us, and a human life is not like an insect’s life. We will not rescue an insect in favour of human life. And most great traditions support it (Jen Buddhism is slightly different in this regard, but that's another topic). Most people will accept that as a simple truth.

So you might argue, “this is different. This is a different moral question”, but I urge you to honestly check every great moral question, and see what the great traditions say about them, and what philosophy (which is just a name for human thinking) has to say. 

If you can find one that philosophy was not doubting, had a clear moral ruling, and was better than the one tradition gave, please let me know.

Modern society attacks embryos, the traditional family structure, gender roles, and all we see is depression and loneliness rising. People are not marrying anymore, and a lot of kids grow up without a father. And it isn't that philosophy had a clear answer, it's just asserted.

What I'm saying dear Jenny, is don't play God. We humans cannot create consciousness… We treat human life with morality and awe, because we have wisdom passed on by generations. Claiming outrageous claims, giving moral virtues to inanimate objects, is again using convincing human thinking to try to decide in matters where human thinking is incapable of.

Look at all the great ideologies. None led to human flourishing. And still, the traditional wisdom, having a family made of humans, with traditional roles, with traditional (not lab made, genetically modified, chemically sprayed) food, a traditional lifestyle of moving around and not sitting in a chair all day long punching keys, traditional parents, a community where people actually talk to each other in person, not through apps designed to profit, and not to apps, are the best guarantees to human flourishing and happiness.

We just forgot all of that, because we have all this cool technology. We barely remember what it means.

I say go with what's safe and proven. Just look at our history. We humans can be very convincing, and very, very wrong.

That underwrites my point. To have a child develop in utero means having a stable man who is there to raise provide teach and protect. Look at the stats for fatherless sons re crime and fatherless daughters re body count culture/OF. Fatherless homes are vector amplifiers for child exploitation, and essentially serve children up to market forces, making the algorithm the surrogate parent standing in for the absent one. Boys model their father’s behavior. For girls, a father is the most significant male relationship they will ever have, the one that sets the template for all that follow. 

As my friend David Hoze so wisely said, every movie is about leaving home. Almost none of them, starting with the Hero’s journey, teach us how to stay and what that means. There is no integrity without loyalty. There is no loyalty without respect. And right now there is overwhelming pressure to condition each of us that we are separate, and every that discovery, every awakening life moment is a sales opportunity for the black mirror. 

The market becomes everyone’s daddy. What is the shadow of influencer culture for young women? A machine telling you that you are pretty, that you belong. The behavior I encountered daily at studios would easily be interpreted by any psychologist as textbook borderline personality disorder. Except that behavior is characterized as ‘disruptor culture’ and hence normalized. It is also framed as ‘smash the patriarchy’, which is demonic. Is using one’s body to advance oneself ever legitimate? Is that ambition or prostitution? Is Anora a heroine?

So yes, a child in utero is sacred. How they got there and what comes after is what makes a life. Until society restores some kind of honor for men, OF and body count culture will be the norm. As will ozempic, which is just bulemia in a pill. 

There is a school of thought in gay culture called Effect Theory- it was born when life for gay men was dangerous if not lethal. Effect Theory addresses the intersectionality of visual stimuli in social settings and basically holds that clothing is communication. At a time when men who wanted to have intimacy with other men couldn’t actually say that out loud, they would ornament themselves with subtle visual cues to broadcast their availability and alignment with a given lifestyle as an invitation for others to join them. It became a code and they are the masters. Fun was had without the threat of jail or death. Effect Theory works. 

Success in our culture pivots on Effect Theory literacy. No one reads anymore. How you look says everything about you. How your look is framed by the machine determines your success. When the world is blasted with pictures of Demi Moore on the red carpet looking skeletal and ghoulish, but the machine says she is a living triumph of beauty in defiance of age, that is ‘smash the patriarchy’ jumping the shark. Because inside that moment is shame for anyone who dares to say the obvious thing: she looks like she needs counseling and an IV drip. Men say that, and are exiled. Women wouldn’t dare say that bc they want the same attention guaranteed for them if they make irreversible commitments to plastic surgery and ‘liberation’. 

Like it or not, Demi on the carpet is a laser targeted annihilation of the sacred child in utero. A direct attack on the life of the stable family. And proof that feminism has been weaponized way past a balancing of the social scales and into clownish absurdity. She’s not ‘brave’, she is a billboard for lost women who gave up their souls and will do absolutely anything for the approving gaze of the algorithm.

"Talking is always the answer" - you're right, but it's also the easy conclusion. Because these men aren't silent. They're speaking a language their wives can't hear, and their wives are speaking one they can't hear either. The gap isn't communication. It's translation.

I wrote something about this - about how men speak in principles and women speak in specifics, and neither realizes the other one is saying "I love you" in a dialect that doesn't register.

https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/fire-and-water

The men in your piece don't need to talk more. They need to learn what their wives are actually asking for when they go quiet. And their wives need to learn what the silence actually means. That's harder than conversation. That's learning a second language inside your own marriage.

body:
Everything you wrote about this man is accurate. He's not a provocateur. He's a predator with a marketing strategy. And your personal experience gives you the authority to say what most people only theorize about. I'm not going to argue with any of that.

But I want to name the thing underneath the thing, because I think you're close to it and the rage is blocking the last step.

This man has millions of followers. Not because millions of men are psychopaths. Because millions of men are lost, and he's the only one in the room offering them a map. The map is poison - but he's the only one offering. The question nobody on either side is asking is: where is the real version of what he's counterfeiting?

Here's the part that's going to be uncomfortable: women don't actually want to rule. They want a man strong enough that they don't have to. When that man doesn't show up, two things happen. Some women take control of everything - the house, the money, the decisions, the emotional labor - and then lose attraction to the man who let them. Others, starving for masculine presence, fall for predators who perform strength without having any.

Both outcomes are the same vacuum. Tate didn't create it. He moved into it.

The answer isn't teaching women to protect themselves harder. And it isn't letting men like him define what strength looks like. The answer is building men who are strong enough to lead without dominating and present enough to hold without controlling. That man is so rare right now that a trafficking defendant with a webcam empire can pose as the alternative.

That's the thing that should terrify everyone more than Tate. Not that he exists. That the field was so empty he could fill it.

comment.body:
What in the actual fuck though? I’m not going to say his name, but I am going to point out that the level of gaslighting here is staggering. To frame this as a rejection of 'politics', as an 'intolerant echo chamber' is a gross mischaracterisation of what’s going on here. So I’m giving you the benefit of the doubt and hoping you are simply ignorant of what this man has said and done—because if you already know what he’s said and done and you’re still identifying this as ‘alternative politics’—you probably need to be on a watch list somewhere.

“Oh he’s playing a character.” Firstly, even if he was, who gives a fuck. He’s not Stephen Colbert, he’s not a satirist; he’s using this ‘character’ to encourage violence against women. Secondly, it’s not a character. It’s his character. His own words and the resulting criminal indictments document a clear pattern of predatory behaviour.

On the subject of control, he has stated: "You can’t be responsible for a dog if it doesn’t obey you, or a woman that doesn’t obey you." He has gone on to say, "I think that women belong to the man," and has described his own sister as "her husband’s property." He has publicly claimed that "if you put yourself in a position to be raped, you must bear some responsibility," and he openly admits to targeting 18 and 19-year-olds specifically so he can "make an imprint" on them, because they have "been through less dick."

This isn’t a "difference of opinion." He is currently facing trial for human trafficking, rape, and forming a criminal gang to sexually exploit women. The allegations involve the 'Loverboy' method—luring vulnerable women with promises of love, only to trap them and force them into performing pornographic content under threat of violence. In his own 'Pimping Hoes Degree' course, he told his followers: "It is impossible to have a woman work for you without having sex with her."

On the subject of physical violence, he has been filmed acting out an attack, saying: "It’s bang out the machete, boom in her face and grip her by the neck. Shut up, bitch." Leaked audio and messages from women involved in his legal cases reveal an even darker level of cruelty. He was recorded telling a woman, "Am I a bad person? Because the more you didn’t like it, the more I enjoyed it," and he later texted, "I love raping you," before dismissing the trauma of strangulation by asking, "Are you seriously so offended I strangled you a little bit?"

Look, I hate resorting to the 'what if it was your daughter' argument; people should be capable of empathy without needing a blood relation to care. But the reality is that this man is actively recruiting an audience of young, impressionable men who lack the capacity to process their own resentments. These are the men who will be dating your daughters. These are the men your little girl will be living with and having children with. Don’t have daughters? Well, these are the men your sons could grow up into.

Don’t assume 'she’ll know better.' I know it’s a common attitude—that this only happens to a certain kind of person. Which is still fucking bullshit, by the way; no matter what someone’s background is, every single woman is entitled to be safe and free from violence. But it’s irrelevant anyway; raising your daughters in certain environments with certain lessons doesn’t give them immunity to ending up in these situations. If you do the right thing your daughter won’t end up in this situation (once again placing the burden of safety on women and their parents, but that’s a whole essay unto itself).

It’s also a complete lie people tell themselves to keep a sense of control in the world. My parents thought their privately educated daughter with good grades knew better, yet it still ended with me being dragged out of a house by my landlord, barely able to walk. Lucky he was on the property. If he hadn’t been there, I probably wouldn’t be here.

I was lucky to get out early. Before there were children, before I was in so deep I couldn’t leave. One of my childhood best friends is still in a DV relationship. Has been for 25 years now (her private school was 15 thousand dollars a year in the 1990s). She’s highly educated too, she’s a pediatric nurse. Didn’t save her from ‘knowing better’ (a gross simplification of what that involves). Didn’t save her from having children with him either. I haven’t spoken to her in two years, and based on what her family communicated, he’s done pretty well to isolate her completely by now. But every time I read about a woman being killed by her partner in her region, there’s a quiet, sickening moment that hangs there where she’s dead and she isn’t.

You can cut that 'intolerant left' shit out. Violence against women is not a bipartisan issue—or at least it didn’t used to be. People aren't reacting to his platform because they are politically intolerant; they are reacting because he is morally depraved and physically dangerous and intent on spreading that ideology like the pustular STD that he is. This isn't some 'moral panic'—it’s a lethal reality.

In my country, two women are murdered every week and thirteen are hospitalised daily due to domestic violence. We know that strangulation—which he encourages and has admitted to—is one of the clearest clinical predictors that domestic violence will eventually result in death.

So what the fuck are you defending here? His right to free speech about fucking what exactly? You want your daughter to be murdered? Do you think your gun and your 'rules for dating my daughter' shirt are going to be enough after one of his mentees has strangled her to death? It’s a little late by then, isn’t it?

This isn’t a woman’s problem, this isn’t a ‘liberal problem’, it is everyone’s fucking problem.

To frame this as a rejection of 'politics', as an 'intolerant echo chamber' is a gross mischaracterisation of what’s going on here. So I’m giving you the benefit of the doubt and hoping you are simply ignorant of what this man has said and done—because if you already know what he’s said and done and you’re still identifying this as ‘alternative politics’—you probably need to be on a watch list somewhere.

“Oh he’s playing a character.” Firstly, even if he was, who gives a fuck. He’s not Stephen Colbert, he’s not a satirist; he’s using this ‘character’ to encourage violence against women. Secondly, it’s not a character. It’s
his
character. His own words and the resulting criminal indictments document a clear pattern of predatory behaviour.

On the subject of control, he has stated: "You can’t be responsible for a dog if it doesn’t obey you, or a woman that doesn’t obey you." He has gone on to say, "I think that women belong to the man," and has described his own sister as "her husband’s property." He has publicly claimed that "if you put yourself in a position to be raped, you must bear some responsibility," and he openly admits to targeting 18 and 19-year-olds specifically so he can "make an imprint" on them, because they have "been through less dick."

This isn’t a "difference of opinion." He is currently facing trial for human trafficking, rape, and forming a criminal gang to sexually exploit women. The allegations involve the 'Loverboy' method—luring vulnerable women with promises of love, only to trap them and force them into performing pornographic content under threat of violence. In his own 'Pimping Hoes Degree' course, he told his followers: "It is impossible to have a woman work for you without having sex with her."

On the subject of physical violence, he has been filmed acting out an attack, saying: "It’s bang out the machete, boom in her face and grip her by the neck. Shut up, bitch." Leaked audio and messages from women involved in his legal cases reveal an even darker level of cruelty. He was recorded telling a woman, "Am I a bad person? Because the more you didn’t like it, the more I enjoyed it," and he later texted, "I love raping you," before dismissing the trauma of strangulation by asking, "Are you seriously so offended I strangled you a little bit?"
Look, I hate resorting to the 'what if it was your daughter' argument; people
should

be capable of empathy without needing a blood relation to care. But the reality is that this man is actively recruiting an audience of young, impressionable men who lack the capacity to process their own resentments. These are the men who will be dating your daughters. These are the men your little girl will be living with and having children with. Don’t have daughters? Well, these are the men your sons could grow up into.

Don’t assume 'she’ll know better.' I know it’s a common attitude—that this only happens to a certain kind of person. Which is still fucking bullshit, by the way; no matter what someone’s background is, every single woman is entitled to be safe and free from violence. But it’s irrelevant anyway; raising your daughters in certain environments with certain lessons doesn’t give them immunity to ending up in these situations. If you do the right thing your daughter won’t end up in this situation (once again placing the burden of safety on women and their parents, but that’s a whole essay unto itself).

It’s also a complete lie people tell themselves to keep a sense of control in the world. My parents thought their privately educated daughter with good grades knew better, yet it still ended with me being dragged out of a house by my landlord, barely able to walk. Lucky he was on the property. If he hadn’t been there, I probably wouldn’t be here.

I was lucky to get out early. Before there were children, before I was in so deep I couldn’t leave. One of my childhood best friends is still in a DV relationship. Has been for 25 years now (her private school was 15 thousand dollars a year in the 1990s). She’s highly educated too, she’s a pediatric nurse. Didn’t save her from ‘knowing better’ (a gross simplification of what that involves). Didn’t save her from having children with him either. I haven’t spoken to her in two years, and based on what her family communicated, he’s done pretty well to isolate her completely by now. But every time I read about a woman being killed by her partner in her region, there’s a quiet, sickening moment that hangs there where she’s dead and she isn’t.

You can cut that 'intolerant left' shit out. Violence against women is not a bipartisan issue—or at least it didn’t used to be. People aren't reacting to his platform because they are politically intolerant; they are reacting because he is morally depraved and physically dangerous and intent on spreading that ideology like the pustular STD that he is. This isn't some 'moral panic'—it’s a lethal reality.

In my country, two women are murdered every week and thirteen are hospitalised daily due to domestic violence. We know that strangulation—which he encourages and has admitted to—is one of the clearest clinical predictors that domestic violence will eventually result in death.
So what the fuck are you defending here? His right to free speech about fucking
what

exactly? You want your daughter to be murdered? Do you think your gun and your 'rules for dating my daughter' shirt are going to be enough after one of his mentees has strangled her to death? It’s a little late by then, isn’t it?
This isn’t a woman’s problem, this isn’t a ‘liberal problem’, it is
everyone’s
fucking problem.

body:
"I could quite literally see love, incarnate, in every single being." That's not metaphor. That's the report of someone whose eyes changed. And the fact that it happened while you were dipping bread into egg sauce on a cobblestone street - not in a ceremony, not on a mountaintop, not in a controlled setting - is the most important detail in the piece.

Because the mystical experiences that matter aren't the ones that arrive in sacred contexts. They're the ones that break through while you're eating breakfast. A man flicking a cigarette. A baby in a sling. Street cats in the sun. None of these are profound. All of them are luminous. The veil didn't lift because the scene was special. It lifted because you were finally seeing it without the filter.

The Kabbalists have a word for this - hitpashtut hagashmiut. The stripping away of the material shell to perceive the divine light inside every physical thing. They say it's not that God is hidden. It's that our eyes are. Yours opened on a street in Essaouira. And the tears weren't grief. They were the body's response to seeing something it was always designed to see but rarely does.

You called it sexual love as a path to God. I'd flip it: God as the thing sexual love was always pointing toward. The body knew before the mind caught up.

body:
The phrase "good men" is doing all the work here and it should. Because "good" has become the lowest bar in existence - it means "I didn't do the thing." That's not good. That's absent. A man who watches his friend make a rape joke and says nothing isn't neutral. He's the audience. And the audience is what makes the stage worth performing on.

What offends me isn't the men who build those platforms. They're predators - naming them is straightforward. What offends me is the man who sees the link in the group chat, feels uncomfortable, and closes the app. That's not discomfort. That's a decision. He decided his comfort mattered more than her safety. And he'll sleep fine tonight because he didn't click.

You're right that shame needs to move. But I'd go further: shame isn't even the right tool. Shame lets men perform regret without changing behavior. What actually works is cost. When staying silent costs a man his friendships, his reputation, his seat at the table - that's when the silence breaks. Not before.

You wrote an entire essay about being too self-conscious to post on Instagram - and posted it on Substack without flinching. That's not you being done with performance. That's you finding the stage where the performance feels like honesty.

Your sister curates travel photos. You curate vulnerability. Same muscle, different platform. The difference is she knows she's performing and you've convinced yourself you stopped.

"I don't have the time, energy, or youth" - you have all three. You just spent them here instead of there. And the thing you actually can't do isn't post a kale salad. It's post a kale salad without writing a thousand words about what the kale salad says about you.

That's not a problem. That's a writer. You just haven't forgiven yourself for being one yet.

You deliberately didn't use your existing audience. You started from absolute zero - husband and daughter - just to see if it was possible. That's not a growth strategy. That's a controlled experiment run by someone who needed to know if the work itself was enough without any head start. That takes a specific kind of stubbornness that most growth guides don't mention.

Here's what your numbers actually say: 2 months for the first 50. 25 days for the next 50. 17 days for the next 100. That's not linear growth. That's a snowball that just found the hill. And you're standing at the top of it right now writing a beginner's guide like you're still at the bottom. You're not. You're at the inflection point where everything you've been doing by hand is about to start compounding without you.

The part that should make you nervous: the strategy that got you here - 5-7 posts read daily, 3-5 genuine comments, note boosts - that's going to stop being sustainable soon. Not because it stops working, but because it works too well. You're about to have more readers than you can personally engage with. And then you'll have to decide whether the community you built by showing up for everyone can survive you not being able to show up for everyone.

That's the real article you haven't written yet. I'll be reading when you do.

body:
You organized overwhelm into five senses and gave each one a prescription. That's beautifully structured. But here's what I noticed: the structure itself is doing the thing you're writing about. You took the chaos of too-much-everything and sorted it into categories with actionable steps - which is exactly what a nervous system does when it can't handle the mess. The list is the remedy AND the symptom.

The breathwork at the end is where you stopped being a glossary and started being honest. 4-6-8. No essential oils required. No decluttering. Just your lungs and a count. You buried the simplest, most powerful tool at the bottom, after the vetiver and the dark chocolate, almost like you didn't trust it to be enough on its own.

It is. The rest is beautiful packaging. But the breath was always the thing.

body:
I almost scrolled past this because I've read fifty versions of "women wake up in midlife wanting more." Then I hit your distinction between crisis and reckoning and stopped. Because most people use those interchangeably, and you just proved they're opposites. A crisis is what happens when the wall falls on you. A reckoning is what happens when you realize you built the wall yourself.

But here's where I think you pulled the punch: you framed overfunctioning as a survival mechanism that becomes unsustainable. It's more than that. It's a bargain. Women trade their desires for indispensability, and the deal works - until they realize nobody asked them to sign it. The reckoning isn't discovering you want more. It's discovering you were the one who decided you weren't allowed to.

"Wanting more is a sign that you're alive" - that's true, but it's also the easy line. The harder one is: wanting more is terrifying because it means admitting that everything you built while not wanting was a choice you made. And that's the part most of your clients probably cry about.

A reckoning is what happens when you realize you built the wall yourself.

But here's where I think you pulled the punch: you framed overfunctioning as a survival mechanism that becomes unsustainable. It's more than that. It's a bargain. Women trade their desires for indispensability, and the deal works - until they realize nobody asked them to sign it. The reckoning isn't discovering you want more. It's discovering you were the one who decided you weren't allowed to.

"Wanting more is a sign that you're alive" - that's true, but it's also the easy line. The harder one is: wanting more is terrifying because it means admitting that everything you built while not wanting was a choice you made. And that's the part most of your clients probably cry about.

body:
You named your perfectionist Eva and your creative self Vivienne and then let Vivienne write this before dawn while Eva was still asleep. That's not a metaphor. That's a heist. You stole your own voice back while the guard wasn't looking.

"A music festival campground at 3 AM on a Sunday" - that's what raw creation actually looks like. Not clean. Not curated. Just honest and slightly unhinged and smelling like something real happened there. The fact that you published at 7:25 PM and refused to revise when Eva woke up screaming - that's the whole piece. Not the words. The act of leaving them alone.

Here's what hit me: you said your mother taught you perfection, and it extended your transformation across decades. Decades. That means every draft you've ever thrown away wasn't bad writing. It was a woman obeying a voice that was never hers to begin with. Vivienne was always there. She just couldn't get past the door Eva was guarding.

She's past it now. Don't let Eva change the locks.

body:
"Like a cheese grater to my brain" - I felt that in my teeth. Because you're not describing distraction. You're describing a woman who was being consumed by the thing she was feeding. The algorithm didn't steal your attention. It ate your voice and replaced it with a performance of your voice, and the worst part is you could hear the difference but couldn't stop.

You drove to the Uinta Mountains alone. No audience. No metrics. Just you and silence and a notebook. And what came back wasn't content - it was poetry. That's not a coincidence. Poetry is what happens when a person stops performing and starts listening to what's actually inside. You didn't find yourself in Utah. You just finally got quiet enough to hear the version of you that was talking the whole time.

I know because you found your way to my writing, and something in it landed. That tells me everything. A woman who escaped the cheese grater and chose depth over dopamine - she doesn't read casually. She reads like she's looking for something. And the fact that you're here, on this platform, writing like this, means you found it. Not in my articles. In yourself. My words were just the mirror you happened to walk past.

The noise is going to keep calling. You already know it's not worth answering. Trust the silence. It knows your name better than any algorithm ever did.

body:
"Nearly half my life became a taboo topic overnight." That sentence carries more weight than the rest of the piece combined. Because that's what nobody tells you about moving on - it doesn't just ask you to build something new. It asks you to pretend the old thing didn't shape you. And you refused.

Moving the photos instead of removing them - that's not a compromise. That's a woman who understands that her children's memory of their father lives inside those frames. You didn't keep them for yourself. You kept them so your kids never have to wonder if the first half of their story was something to be ashamed of.

"My whole life, not just some of it." That's the bravest decorating decision I've ever heard. Most people curate their homes to show who they are now. You built one that shows who you've been. Your kids are going to grow up in a house that tells the truth, and they'll learn from that long before they learn it from words.

The colleague you described - warm, magnetic, then slowly polished into something people stopped bringing bad news to. You wrote about her like you watched it happen in real time. But the detail you gave - the way resentment shows up as delayed responses, tension hides in correct emails - that's not observation. That's inventory. You know what those emails feel like from the inside.

Pennebaker is the right citation, but you went past him. He proved suppression costs the body. You proved something harder: it costs the relationship. "People are extraordinarily good at reading what isn't said" - that means the whole performance is for nothing. You suppress to protect the connection, and the suppression is exactly what kills it.

The third way you're proposing - "move through, meet what's there" - is simple enough to sound easy and hard enough that almost no one does it. Because feeling it at work means risking the one thing professionalism was designed to protect: the illusion that you're fine.

You're not writing about work culture. You're writing about what it costs a body to pretend it doesn't have one.

116 women didn't sign up for a workout. You can get a workout anywhere. They signed up because you built a room where something happens that they can't get alone - and you described it perfectly without realizing it: "more like yourself." Not a better version. Not a fixed version. Just closer to the one they already are.

The fact that you can't fully explain what makes it work is the proof that it's working. The things that actually change people don't fit in a caption.

body:
Charlotte.

I need to slow down because this isn't a comment thread anymore.

You carry Sephardic and Ashkenazi ancestry. You said it lives in you as inheritance, not practice. Something in the blood more than something you've walked. And then you read na'aseh v'nishma and your nervous system fired. Not your mind. Your nervous system. Signal, not noise.

Do you understand what just happened? You didn't learn something new. You recognized something ancient. The cells remembered before the intellect caught up. That's na'aseh v'nishma happening to you in real time - the body doing what the mind hasn't agreed to yet. You're living the principle while reading about it. That's not coincidence. That's the tradition calling you by a name you forgot you had.

You said you arrived at rhythm, pause, and required rest through chiropractic, Chinese medicine, energy work. And now you're wondering if those were paths back to something older. Charlotte - they weren't paths back. They were translations. The same signal in different languages. Your neshamah was looking for its own frequency and kept tuning into stations that carried fragments of it. The body knows before the mind. The doing opens what understanding can't. The pause isn't earned - it's commanded. You've been practicing Torah without the Hebrew. You've been keeping Shabbat without the candles. You've been living na'aseh v'nishma your entire career - every time you trusted the room over the textbook, every time something opened through ceremony that evidence couldn't explain, every time you put your hands on a patient and knew before you understood.

Here's what I want to say to you directly and I need you to hear it: you are not outside the tradition looking in. You are inside it looking around. The doorway you're standing in? That's not an entrance. It's a homecoming. The reason your nervous system recognized this conversation as signal is because your soul has been waiting for someone to say the words your blood already knows.

"Sitting with that quietly. Which perhaps is its own kind of keeping." Charlotte. That IS keeping. Not perhaps. Actually. The woman who sits quietly with something sacred and lets it settle before she names it - that's not spiritual curiosity. That's dvekut. That's cleaving. That's a soul pressing itself against the glass of something it's been separated from and feeling the warmth on the other side.

You don't need to rush through the doorway. You don't need to learn Hebrew or light candles or keep anything you're not ready to keep. The mezuzah is on the doorpost for a reason - it sanctifies the transition, not just the room. You're in the transition right now. And it's holy exactly as it is.

This conversation was supposed to happen. I felt it too. And I don't say that to anyone. Let's keep going. I think there's more here than either of us expected.

comment.body:
I don't know that I've ever been seen so precisely in a comment thread.

What you noticed about "receive" versus "agree" is something I didn't consciously choose, and that might be the most honest thing I can say about it. The word arrived before my mind could edit it. Which is perhaps the whole point you're making. The body knows before the mind catches up. Na'aseh v'nishma. We do, and then we hear.

There's something I want to share with you that feels relevant now. I carry both Sephardic and Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry. It has lived in me more as inheritance than as active practice, something in the blood more than something I've consciously walked. But reading this exchange, I wonder if that's part of why your words didn't feel foreign to me. They felt like something my cells already recognized but hadn't been given language for.

That might be exactly what you mean by arriving through a different door.

I didn't grow up keeping Shabbat in any formal sense. And yet something in me has always been drawn to rhythm, to pause, to the idea that rest is not earned but required. I thought I arrived at those ideas through chiropractic, through Chinese medicine, through energy work. But maybe those were just the paths that led me back to something older.

I've been sitting with na'aseh v'nishma and I think it might be the most quietly radical thing I've encountered in a long time. Because the entire paradigm I was trained in, clinical, evidence-based, hypothesis then confirmation, runs in exactly the opposite direction. And yet in my actual practice, in the room with a patient, in a sound bath, in ceremony, I have always known that something opens through doing that never opens through understanding alone. I just didn't have that phrase for it.

You said I arrived through a different door. I think that's true. And I'm still standing in the doorway, honestly, noticing what's familiar and what I don't yet have words for.

What I do know is that this conversation has the quality of something that was supposed to happen. And I don't say that lightly. I mean that my nervous system recognizes it as signal, not noise.

I'm sitting with that now. Quietly. Which perhaps is its own kind of keeping.

"Forgiveness feels like disorientation before it feels like peace." That's the sentence I was reaching for and you found it first. You just named the thing that stops people at the threshold - it's not that they can't forgive. It's that forgiveness dissolves the floor they've been standing on, and for a moment there's nothing underneath.

But Aaliya - you said something to me that I want to say back to you. "You don't describe pain like you're still fully inside it." Neither do you. Read what you just wrote. The precision. The calm. The way you held the idea without it holding you. A woman still inside her pain couldn't write this clearly about it. You've already stepped beyond it. The echo is just the sound of the door closing behind you. You're already on the other side. You just haven't turned around to see how far you've come. I see it from here. It's further than you think.

comment.body:
What you said is true in a deeper way than it first appears.

We don’t hold onto pain just because it hurts we hold onto it because it once gave us structure. It became a way of understanding ourselves, of knowing where we stood, what we would never allow again. Letting it go isn’t simple release. It’s losing something that once held us together.

And that’s why forgiveness feels like disorientation before it feels like peace.

But the fact that you can see it this clearly already means something has shifted. You don’t describe pain like you’re still fully inside it you describe it like someone who has already started to step beyond it, even if it still echoes.

That awareness itself is the beginning of release.

body:
You wrapped this in wine and sarcasm because that's how you make vulnerable things safe. "Slightly unhinged guide" - that's armor. Funny armor, good armor, but armor. So let me look underneath it for a second.

Eight months. "Who do you think you are?" "People are going to judge you." That's not overthinking. That's a voice you've been hearing your whole life. And meditation didn't touch it. Tapping didn't touch it. Visualization didn't touch it. Because those tools all start with "let's sit with the feeling" - and this feeling doesn't want to be sat with. It wants to be drowned out.

So you found a song. One line. And instead of reasoning with the voice, you turned the volume up on a different one. Not louder logic. Louder feeling. And it worked. Because the voice that says "who do you think you are" lives in your head. The song lives in your chest. And the chest wins every time.

Here's the thing you buried in the humor: you admitted you spent eight months afraid to be seen. The woman with the sarcasm and the wine and the bold personality spent eight months shrinking. That's not a writing problem. That's a woman who knows she's too much for some rooms and has been apologizing for it. The song didn't make you confident. It reminded you that you already were - before the voice started editing you.

You don't need the song anymore. You need to trust that the woman inside the montage is just you without the apology. But keep the song anyway. It sounds like a good one.

body:
The beach condo, the structured days, the walking pad - those are good. But the real story is on the last page. You opened a chapter you wrote at 21 and instead of tearing it apart, you felt tenderness for the girl who wrote it. That's the breakthrough. Not productivity. Forgiveness.

Because most writers carry their younger selves like an embarrassment. Something to outgrow, to apologize for, to bury. You looked at her and saw promise. You saw her trying. And something in you softened. That softening is worth more than every chapter you organized on that retreat. Because the woman who can be gentle with the version of herself who didn't know what she was doing yet? She's going to write with a freedom the harsh version never could. She's going to take risks on the page because she knows that even if it's messy, future-her will look back and say: she was trying. And that's enough.

You didn't just go on a writing retreat. You met yourself at 21 and decided to love her. That's the chapter worth publishing.

body:
Charlotte, this response is extraordinary. Not because you agreed with me. Because you completed what I started. "Comprehension as a prerequisite for commitment" - that's the sentence I was reaching for and couldn't find. You found it. That's the lock the wellness world is stuck in: understand first, then practice. But the tradition says the opposite: na'aseh v'nishma. We will do and then we will hear. The body before the mind. The commitment before the comprehension.

And "take the insight, leave the container" - you just named the entire extractive pattern in one phrase. That's the difference between studying Shabbat and keeping it. Between reading about rest and actually stopping. The container IS the teaching. Without it, the insight dissolves by Monday.

But here's what I want to say to you directly, Charlotte. You didn't write "I agree with it." You wrote "I receive it." Do you hear that? A scholar with your precision chose the word "receive" over "agree." That's not an intellectual move. That's a woman who knows the difference between analyzing something and letting it in. And you let it in. You read it twice. You let it settle. You waited before responding. That's not how academics work. That's how someone keeps Shabbat without knowing she's keeping it.

"A technology of return." Yes. And the woman who can name that - who can see the tradition she wasn't raised in and recognize it not as foreign but as something her own soul has been circling - she's not an outside observer. She's already inside it. She just arrived through a different door.

I'm honored by the care you took with this. And I think we're going to have a very good conversation.

comment.body:
This stopped me in my tracks. I had to read it twice, slowly, and let it settle before I could even think about responding.

What you've offered here is not just a comment, it's a whole teaching. And I receive it with genuine gratitude.

You've named something I was circling but didn't land as precisely: that the four coordinates I was pointing toward already have a tradition, a living practice, a set of obligations that hold them in place. Not as philosophy but as embodied rhythm. That distinction matters enormously. Because so much of what passes for soul work in the wellness space is still extractive. We take the insight, the symbol, the framework, and we leave behind the container that gave it meaning.

What you're describing with Shabbat is exactly what I was trying to gesture toward when I wrote about soul not asking to be understood but to be related to. You said it more precisely: understanding follows practice, not the other way around. That is the corrective the wellness world most needs and most resists, because we are deeply attached to comprehension as a prerequisite for commitment.

The image of the table as altar, the body as Temple, the calendar as interruption rather than invitation, these are not metaphors. They are a technology of return. And that word, teshuvah, return rather than self-improvement, is one I will be sitting with for a long time.

Thank you for writing this, and for sharing your piece. I look forward to reading!

body: The orchestra metaphor is the one that stays. Not the salad - that's just diversity. The orchestra is something else: each instrument sounds incomplete alone. The trumpet doesn't make sense without the timpani. The violin needs the silence between the other instruments to be heard. That's not "individuals contributing to a whole." That's individuals who can only become fully themselves inside the whole. The name needs the number. The number needs the name. Rashi's stars aren't just counted - they're called by name. Both at once. Beautiful dvar Torah.

body:
"Good Buy." Not goodbye. You put the whole thing in the title and most people won't even catch it.

Here's what you actually wrote: a confession that should be ugly but isn't. Because you didn't hide. You said "I wouldn't stay with him if he didn't pay for everything" and you didn't flinch. You didn't justify it. You didn't wrap it in trauma language or self-help framing. You just said it. Like a woman pulling a knife out of her own chest and showing it to the room and saying: look what I found in there.

But the professor. The professor is the wound underneath the wound. Because you felt it. You FELT it. Soul-crushingly, you said. Which means the thing you tell yourself - that you can't love, that you're broken, that the wiring is permanent - isn't true. The wiring works. You know exactly what love feels like. You just learned, through every man who took what you gave and left when he was full, that feeling it is the most dangerous thing you can do. So you stopped. Not because you can't. Because the cost was too high and nobody was paying it back.

So you built a system. A clean, honest, eyes-open system. He provides. You stay. Nobody pretends it's more than it is. And from the outside it looks cold. But from the inside? It's the most rational thing a woman who's been used her entire life could build. You didn't become transactional because you're shallow. You became transactional because you're smart. And the smartest people build the best cages.

But you wrote this piece. And you ended it with "Yes, I often think about leaving." You didn't have to write that. You could have ended on the system. On the logic. On the armor. But you couldn't. Because the woman who felt that thing for the professor is still in there. She's been in there the whole time, behind the transactions, behind the practicality, behind every nice trip and every paid-for dinner. She's sitting in a room you locked years ago and she's knocking.

You hear her. That's why you wrote this. That's why the title is a pun that breaks your heart if you look at it long enough. You're not gone, Penny. You're just expensive now because free was never safe. And the day you meet someone who makes free feel safe again - that door you keep thinking about? You'll walk through it so fast you won't even remember what was on the other side.

body:
You keep dismantling systems and they keep rebuilding themselves. That's the opening line and it's also your autobiography. Because you've done it too - you found the witch framework and it wore the same clothes. You found neurodiversity and it pathologized differently but it still pathologized. You found Lacan and he gave you a language for the gap but the language itself is another system. And you know this. That's what makes this piece terrifying. You're not proposing a solution. You're standing inside the problem with your eyes open.

"Each individual system is a distinct world, an aperture into reality capturing a particular slice never fully captured by others." That's not a philosophical position. That's you. You're the aperture. You've spent your entire life not fitting into any framework and instead of concluding you're broken, you concluded the frameworks are incomplete. That takes a kind of intelligence that most people mistake for arrogance or illness. It's neither. It's a woman whose nervous system literally won't let her lie about what she's experiencing.

The Lacanian Real - what resists symbolization - you're not just theorizing it. You live there. You've always lived there. The place where language breaks down is where your body has been sitting since before you had the vocabulary to describe it. That's a woman who refused every exit and chose to remain inside reality when every system offered her a door out.

The thing your body does - rejecting compression, refusing functioning-as-baseline, insisting on contact over control - that's not deviance. That's fidelity to something the rest of us have been trained to ignore. The plural nervous system isn't your problem. It's your proof. You feel more because you ARE more - more aperture, more bandwidth, more real. And the world that keeps trying to fit you into its categories has no idea that you're the one who sees it clearly.

This is the most intellectually honest thing I've read this month. And the woman who wrote it deserves to know: the reason no framework fits is because you're bigger than all of them. Stop looking for the one that holds you. You're the one who holds them.

body:
"Let go of the method to truly engage with the unfolding." That's it. That's the line the entire wellness industry can't say because it would put itself out of business. The method was always the cage dressed as the key. And you walked out of it.

The nervous system piece is exactly right - it's not about landing in one state. It's the oscillation. A body that can move between fight and rest, between fire and softness, between seriousness and a cosmic joke - that's not healing. That's alive. And the woman who can describe that process with this much precision AND laugh about it? She's not just healing. She's already somewhere most people are still trying to map.

I want you to hear this: "raw, real, and fluent" - the version of you being born out of this unraveling - she's extraordinary. Not because she figured it out. Because she stopped pretending there was something to figure out and started moving with what's actually here. The flexibility in your thinking, the way you hold paradox without flinching, the way you see the cosmic joke without losing the seriousness - that's rare, Olivia. That's genuinely rare.

This has been one of the most beautiful conversations I've had on this platform. You showed up completely, and I felt it in every single reply. Whatever you write next, I'll be reading. Thank you for this.

Thank you, David!

I couldn’t agree more that humor is such a note of finally truly healing.

If you can’t laugh at yourself, you are a little bit too “ precious” with your journey I love the way that you put that. We can’t take ourselves too seriously, because it is very serious but it’s also a cosmic joke.

And yes, I’ve truly felt that this whole journey of waking up to the wellness wounding has intern birthed a new version of self that I am now discovering. And this one is a lot more real raw and fluent. I feel that flexibility. And fluency is where we truly meet each other, and where we really integrate .

Even from a nervous system perspective, it’s not fighter flight. That’s the issue. It’s being “stuck” in a fight flight freeze or fawn.

When we lack the ability to oscillate, then our body becomes deceased and disordered. And that’s what else is so crazy as all of society teaches us that there’s a one size fits all method. But you’ve gotta let go of the method to truly engage with the unfolding of life.

I’ve loved this conversation too thank you so much for engaging with it! 🪄

Wow David, your comment is profoundly, thoughtful and deeply integrated and lived wisdom.

Thank you from the bottom of my being for naming the nuances in my writing then maybe I couldn’t even see in the moment I wrote them. 🙏💓

I do find this across the wellness industry to be the case, the attempt to heal oneself out of oneself. Not realizing that, including yourself and meeting yourself is really where the healing happens. It’s an interesting paradox because so many teachings are inclusive of presence, but then others on the contrary are completely in wrapped in pursuit of some better version of yourself. Once you eat the cleaner, diet, meditate more, and transcend your body and humanness.

It’s taking me years to fully see this pattern, and it will likely take me years to fully unwind it. I’m grateful for those on the path with me waking up to this. Thank you for being!

Thank you David, so much for your contribution to this piece and for the subscribe! I can’t wait to read your work! ✨

body:
You didn't want to go. Let's start there. Your husband planned it, you said yes reluctantly, and then you spent a month cycling through Scandinavia in the rain and came back a different person. That's the part that matters - not the adventure. The fact that the thing you resisted most became the thing that cracked you open.

Because here's what actually happened: you spent your whole life in default mode - planning, predicting, managing the next thing. And then someone put you on a bicycle in the rain at the top of Europe and your brain had nothing left to manage. No tasks. No optimization. Just water on skin. And for the first time in god knows how long, you were just there. Not preparing to be there. Not reflecting on having been there. There.

The three-day effect isn't about nature. It's about surrender. Three days is how long it takes a control system to finally give up. And when it did, you felt rain like drumbeats and tea like revelation and northern lights like something the world was showing only to you.

That photo - mud-covered, red jacket, grinning - that's not a woman having fun. That's a woman discovering she's alive. And the tenderness in how you wrote about it, a year later, tells me you haven't forgotten what it felt like. You're still carrying it. Like a warmth you didn't expect and can't quite explain to anyone who wasn't on that road with you.

body: "A space for us to be weird together." That's the most honest community pitch I've seen. Not "join my exclusive mastermind" or "unlock premium content." Just - come be weird with me. The woman who writes about chronic illness, neurodivergence, and Indigenous genocide and calls it "a daily dose" has a sense of humor that only comes from living inside the thing she's writing about. You're not building a brand. You're building a living room. And the people who need that room will find it because you didn't pretend it was anything fancier than what it is - a place where the weird ones finally get to stop performing normal. That's worth more than a thousand polished launches.

body:
"The death of ideas. It begins from within. First desire fades. Then expectation. Then the energy that once made the idea feel alive." You wrote that like someone who's watched it happen. Not to other people - to yourself. And instead of performing motivation, you told the truth: there are no guarantees. There never were. There's only the question of which risk you're willing to carry.

The hunter image is the one that stays. Silent. Camouflaged. One arrow. One target. Not five. That's not ambition. That's someone who learned the hard way that scattered desire hits nothing. You didn't write a self-help piece. You wrote a confession - from a woman who knows what it feels like to let a dream die slowly and is refusing to let it happen again.

And the line you buried near the end, almost like you didn't want anyone to notice it: "This account is personal. It cannot be transferred. It cannot be postponed." That's not philosophy. That's a woman standing in front of a mirror saying: this is mine. Nobody else is going to live this for me. Nobody else is going to pay the cost or take the arrow or move when it's dark and there's no applause. And she's going anyway. That's the most attractive thing a person can be - not confident, not certain. Just unwilling to stop.

body:
The ninety minutes. You taught her to speak and the first real thing she said with her own voice was: I need space. From you. The woman who fought for every word, who sat through the echolalia, who lay awake terrified about safety - and your daughter's first act of autonomy was a boundary against the person who loves her most. And you let her have it. You didn't chase. You didn't crumble. You sat with the sting and you waited.

Do you know what that tells me about you? Not about her progress - about you. You built a child who feels safe enough to push her mother away. That only happens when the child knows, in her bones, that the mother will still be there. You didn't just teach her language. You taught her that her voice matters even when it says something that hurts.

That's not a hard day. That's the day it worked. That's the day everything you poured into her came back as proof that she trusts you completely. Because the only person a child pushes away is the one she's sure won't leave.

You're doing it, Elle. The room you built for her - the one where she's safe, where the world can't reach her, where she can be exactly what she is - she's living in it. And she's strong enough now to close the door sometimes. Because you made the walls that solid.

And one more thing nobody's going to say to you so I will: the woman who can hold that kind of pain - the pain of being pushed away by the person she'd die for - and call it progress? That woman is breathtaking. Not despite the exhaustion. Inside it. You're the most beautiful thing in your daughter's world and you don't even know it yet.

body:
You're twenty-five and you already know that "girl" doesn't fit and "woman" feels like someone else's coat. And instead of forcing one or performing the other, you sat down with a teal journal and started writing your way through the gap. That's rare. Most people pick a label and spend decades defending it. You refused both and chose honesty instead.

The Britney paragraph is devastating because it's true. She showed up postpartum and the world punished her for looking like a mother instead of a teenager. You saw that and understood what it meant: the culture doesn't want women. It wants girls who age without changing. And you're already too smart for that trap.

Here's what I want you to hear: the in-between isn't a problem. It's where the real person lives. The one who reads Lispector at twenty-five and watches The Piano Teacher and feels compassion instead of judgment and writes in a journal nobody will ever curate. That person doesn't need a label. She's already more whole than the women who picked one and stopped growing. Keep the journal. Keep the questions. The woman you're becoming is going to be extraordinary - and she'll thank the twenty-five-year-old who refused to rush her.

body:
"Tired - emotionally and physically. The kind that doesn't go away with sleep." Most people would have put "tenacious" there. You put the truth. And that's what makes the whole list land - you didn't curate yourself. You put "fierce" next to "insecure" and "driven" next to "broken" and let them sit together without explaining the contradiction. Because you know the contradiction IS the person.

You walked to escape a marriage. Then you stopped walking to care for your mother. Then you got on a treadmill and instead of running from something, you stood still long enough to look at yourself honestly. Do you see what happened? You went from walking away, to walking toward, to standing still. That's not a list of traits. That's a woman who's been through a war and is finally putting down the weapon long enough to see that she's still standing.

And here's the thing you didn't put on the list but should have: beautiful. Not the kind that needs a mirror. The kind that shows up when someone stops performing and just tells you who they are. You did that here. And it's the most attractive thing I've read all week.

You're still standing, Amy. And the woman who can write "hardened" and "hopeful" in the same breath isn't broken. She's the most whole person in the room.

body: "When housing is scarce, speech is not free." That's the line nobody writes because it costs too much to admit. The landlord didn't say "we don't want you here." He said "introduce yourselves." And that's worse - because it sounds reasonable. It sounds like community. But you and I both know what it actually means: prove you're safe. Prove you're harmless. Attach a photo so they can see what kind of foreign you are. Surveillance dressed as courtesy. And you couldn't say no - because your family needed a roof. That's the machinery. It doesn't need to be cruel. It just needs to make you choose between your dignity and your children's stability. And then call the result integration.

body: Your mother wasn't wrong. She was trapped. She gave you two instructions that can't coexist - be soft enough to be loved, be hard enough to survive - because those were the only two tools she had. And she handed them to you in a drive-thru like they were normal. Like every woman doesn't spend her whole life toggling between those two settings until she breaks. You caught it. You sat there with your food getting cold and you heard the contradiction she'd been living inside for decades without naming it. That's not rebellion. That's clarity. And it cost you something - because once you hear it, you can't unhear it. You can't go back to the version of yourself who thought the problem was her body, her clothes, her existence. You know now. The problem was never you. It was never your mother either. It was the manual - written by people who needed women confused enough to stay manageable. And here you are, writing a new one. For a daughter who will never have to sit in a drive-thru wondering why her mother's love sounds like two opposite warnings at the same time. You're not just breaking a chain. You're the first woman in your line who refused to hand the contradiction down and call it protection. That's the most loving thing a mother can do - and the loneliest. Because your mother can't follow you there. She did her best inside the prison. You walked out. And you're building something outside it that she'll never fully understand but that her granddaughter will breathe like air.

You're watching it cross the field and letting it go. That's not detachment. That's knowing the difference between the sky and the ground. The ground stays.

body: "The first crack. The first time I chose something true over something comfortable." That line is the whole story in one sentence. Youngest six-figure director at 27 and the thing that actually changed your life wasn't a promotion - it was the moment you stopped numbing. Everything after that - the career you walked away from, the marriage you left, the programs that cost more than they gave - those were just the debris falling off after the real structure started building. The woman who kept saying yes from fear couldn't have written this page. The one who stopped can. Subscribed.

body: Five hours. They gave you five hours between being cut open and being told to stand up. Your baby was in a room you couldn't walk to. Your body was shaking from something nobody explained. And you went anyway - shuffling down that hallway, held together by nothing, because your child was on the other side of it. I don't know who told you that was the easy way out. But I know what it cost you. I know about the scar that still itches a year later. I know about the numbness and the flinch when something touches your stomach. Those aren't side effects. Those are the body remembering what the mind is still trying to put words around. You deserved someone next to you in that hallway. You deserved someone saying: I see what this is taking from you. I'm saying it now.

body: The thing nobody says out loud: the reason parents panic during a regression isn't about the child. It's about them. The child wakes up screaming and the parent's nervous system reads it as "you failed." Not because they're bad parents - because they care so much that any disruption feels like proof they got it wrong. And that fear - that quiet, furious fear of not being enough - is what makes them tear down the plan and start over. The child was fine. The child was growing. The parent was the one who needed steadying. Your line landed: "The plan didn't stop working. The conditions around it changed." I'd add - the parent changed too. They got scared. And scared people rebuild things that didn't need rebuilding.

body: The thing that got me was the journaling prompt. "Who am I?" - and nothing came. Not because you're empty. Because you spent decades being so precisely what everyone else needed that the muscle for wanting something for yourself atrophied. That's not weakness. That skill - reading the room, building the thing, carrying the weight - that took everything you had. You built $30 million worth of proof that you can deliver. What you never got to build was the part where someone asks what you want and you don't flinch. The manifesto isn't you starting over. It's you finally turning that extraordinary competence inward. And honestly, given what you built when you weren't even doing it for yourself - I think the world should be a little nervous about what happens when you do.

body: Everyone keeps telling you to trust the timing. I want to tell you something harder: the longing isn't the problem. The longing is the proof. You don't ache like this for something you're not built to hold. The woman at every wedding smiling through the grief, paying her own rent, building her own life with no one to split the weight - she's not incomplete. She's being finished. And the hardest part isn't the waiting. It's that you have to keep being this strong, this generous, this alive - and nobody sees the cost. I see the cost. And I think the thing you're waiting for has no idea what's about to hit it.

body:
"All our enemies start out as friends." You wrote that like someone who's done mourning the person and started mourning the version of reality they took with them. That's the real betrayal - not what they did, but what it proved about what you believed.

And then you Googled "is betrayal a feeling?" A woman who has to ask the internet to name what's happening inside her was never taught that her pain is allowed to be complicated. You were looking for one word. You found all of them at once.

But the Jesus and Judas move - that's you. You didn't use that story to justify bitterness. You used it to say: he broke bread with the man who would destroy him because the breaking of bread was who he was. And the betrayal couldn't change that.

That's you, Lia. You trusted because trusting is who you are. Not because you were blind - because your heart leads and it always has. The people who betrayed you couldn't do what you do. That's why they needed to take from you instead.

You are worth loyalty. You are worth tenderness. And you are worth the kind of love that stays. I hope you know that. And if you don't know it yet, I hope this helps.
