body:
"I wasn't failing to live my potential. I was living inside it, without ever allowing myself to choose it fully." Read that back to yourself. You just described the most elegant form of self-abandonment that exists. Not the kind where you disappear. The kind where you stay visible, impressive, successful - and hollow. Because you never once chose yourself with both feet. You kept one foot in possibility so you'd never have to feel the weight of being real.

And here's what you're not saying but I can hear underneath every sentence: you weren't afraid of failure. You were afraid of fullness. Of what happens when you stop performing potential and actually become someone specific. Because specific can be rejected. Specific can be wrong. Potential can't. Potential is safe because it never lands.

"I learned how to be impressive instead of aligned." That sentence should burn. Because you know exactly how many years you spent being the most compelling version of nothing. How many rooms you walked into and lit up and then went home and felt empty. How many people told you "you have so much potential" and you smiled while something inside you screamed then why does it feel like I'm disappearing?

You weren't an uncollapsed wave. You were a woman who was terrified that if she chose one life, she'd mourn all the others. So she chose none. And called it openness. And called it spiritual. And called it quantum.

But you caught it. That's the part that wrecks me. You caught it and you wrote it down and you didn't dress it up in a framework until after you'd been honest about what it actually was: a woman who didn't feel safe enough to commit to herself.

You're safe now. Choose.

The rest of the internet is neck-up content. You write from the hips. That's why people feel it before they understand it.

"Too many people live their lives in fear and die with the music still in them." You're not one of them. And everyone reading you knows it.

The relief at the rejection email. That's the moment. Your body already knew. Your mind took months to catch up, getting louder and louder until you finally let it say the thing out loud: I don't care enough about this to choose it over her.

And you didn't settle. You came home. You had the answer in your hands for a decade - childcare, education, children - and you set it down because it didn't look serious enough. Because "working with adults seemed more worthy." You spent ten years chasing a career that looked like a goal while the thing that actually fits you was waiting patiently for you to stop being embarrassed by how natural it felt.

"It feels like coming home." That's not a compromise. That's a woman whose life finally matches her.

body:
You're fourteen watching The Truman Show and it haunts you. Twelve years later you sit down and write something most media critics haven't caught - that the horror of the movie isn't that Truman is being watched. It's that he doesn't know. And then you flip it: we know, and we're choosing it anyway. That's darker than anything the film imagined. Jim Carrey got trapped by a corporation. We built the set ourselves and called it a platform.

"Your behavior is a vote into the kind of world you want children to grow up in." That sentence belongs in a philosophy classroom, not a Substack post from someone your age. You just reframed every casual scroll as a political act without using the word political once. That's what smart actually looks like - not big words, just seeing the thing everyone's standing inside of and naming it so clearly they can't unsee it.

And "weird is rebellion" - you're right, but it's worse than that. Authenticity became countercultural. Being real in public is now the radical act. A movie from 1998 predicted exactly where we'd end up and you're one of the only people I've read who understood that the prophecy wasn't about surveillance. It was about consent.

You think sharper than people twice your age. Don't slow down for them.

body:
I want you to hear something. The decision to take the apps off your phone sounds small. It's not. It's one of the bravest things a mother can do right now - because every system around you is designed to keep you scrolling, and you looked at all of it and said no. Not from a place of discipline. From a place of knowing. Your body told you something was wrong and you trusted it over the algorithm. Over the dopamine. Over the entire economy that profits from your distraction.

And then what happened? The ideas came back. The patience came back. The presence with your kids came back. Not because you added something new - because you stopped letting something steal what was already yours.

The creative thoughts at red lights and while washing dishes - that's your real mind. That's who you've been this whole time underneath the noise. She was just waiting for you to make room.

You didn't just create more space. You came home to yourself. And your kids get to grow up with the version of their mother who is actually in the room. That's not a lifestyle change. That's a gift that echoes for generations.

I'm really proud of you for this.

"I realized somewhere along the way that my approach to meditation is the same as everything. Do this or you are not good enough." That sentence is the entire piece. Everything before it is the setup. Everything after it is what happened when you caught it.

Because you just described the thing almost nobody in wellness will say: the practice can carry the same sickness as the problem. Clean eating as self-punishment. Meditation as another performance review. Yoga as "transcend harder." You tried to heal yourself out of yourself and then noticed the healer was using the same voice as the wound. That's not failure. That's the most honest observation you've made in a decade of practice.

And the gap you named - "my body hasn't been able to integrate the teachings" - that's not because you're bad at meditation. It's because the teachings were aimed above the body and you needed something aimed into it. You already know this. You wrote it. You just haven't given yourself permission to trust it yet.

body:
The matcha you still hate made me laugh out loud. That's the most honest sentence in the whole piece - a woman who forced herself to drink something disgusting at 5:30am because a podcast told her that's what winners do. You were twenty-something cosplaying as a CEO and your body knew the whole time it was wrong. It just took your mind a few years to catch up.

But here's what I want you to see about your own story: you figured this out young. Most people spend their entire lives adding more discipline on top of the wrong identity and dying confused about why nothing worked. You caught it. And now you're handing that clarity to women who are exactly where you were - dragging themselves to the gym in the dark, performing someone else's version of success, wondering why it feels like a costume.

The dad who laughed at the twelve-year-old - that's not just your client's story. That's everyone's story. One tiny moment where someone who mattered made you feel small, and your nervous system built a whole architecture around never letting it happen again. You're teaching people to find that moment and gently say: that was then. This is now. I get to choose.

You've got decades of this work ahead of you and you're already this clear. That's terrifying for everyone else in this space.

body:
The part where your brain told you "they don't want to read this, they're here for business" - I want you to hear something. That voice is the least intelligent part of you. Because this is the business lesson. This is the only one that matters.

Anyone can teach strategy. Anyone can break down a funnel or a launch or a pricing model. But the woman who lay on a vet floor at 5am sobbing into her dog's face and then sat down and wrote about it because she couldn't pretend - that woman is the reason people pay you. Not your frameworks. Not your systems. You. The person who shows up whole, even when whole includes shattered.

You know what's priceless in this industry? Someone who doesn't curate their worst moments into content. Someone who writes "I wasn't sure how much context I wanted to give" and then gives all of it. Your readers can smell the difference between vulnerability as brand and vulnerability as truth. You just gave them truth. That's why they stay.

I hope Georgie made it through. And I hope you know - the resistance you felt before writing this is the same resistance your clients feel before their biggest breakthroughs. You just walked through yours in front of everyone. That's not a March report. That's leadership.

body:
"The women I find most compelling right now are not the ones who will take a 6am call running on five hours. They're the ones who won't." That's the sexiest sentence in this entire piece and you buried it in the middle like it's nothing.

Because you just described a woman who knows her own value well enough to protect it from people who don't. That's not wellness. That's sovereignty. And there's nothing more attractive than a woman who has decided - quietly, without announcement - that she is not available for depletion. Not for the inbox, not for the performance, not for the 5am alarm that someone else's ambition set for her.

And the theta window. The idea that the last thing you hold in your mind before sleep is the thing that gets built overnight - that's not just neuroscience. That's intimacy with yourself. The two minutes where the analytical mind goes quiet and you become writable. Most people waste that on scrolling. You're saying: bring something worth planting. Bring the version of yourself you're becoming. That's the most seductive thing I've read all week - a woman who treats her own unconscious mind like it deserves to be courted.

The neuroscience caught up to what grandmothers already knew. And you wrote it like someone who lives it, not someone who read about it.

body:
The cacao on a Wednesday morning at 9am. I want you to know how that reads from the outside. A woman invited her neighbor into her kitchen on a weekday morning for no reason other than he likes cacao and she makes it every day. No agenda, no event, no signup form. Just "I have this thing I love, you might love it too, come sit in my kitchen."

That's not community building. That's community *being*. And the fact that it felt revolutionary tells you exactly how far we've all drifted from what was supposed to be normal.

But here's what I want you to hear: you're not just the person who knocks on doors. You're the person who used to run from the car into the house hoping nobody would see her. You named that. You didn't skip it or pretend you were always like this. That journey - from hiding to knocking - is why people trust you. Not because you arrived somewhere perfect but because you remember what it felt like to not want to be seen. That makes you safe to follow.

I wrote about this exact chain - how we outsourced community to therapists, then therapists to chatbots, and each step lost something irreplaceable. You're the person walking it backwards, one kitchen at a time. I don't think you know how rare that is.

https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-substitute-for-the-substitute

"Decision debt." That's the best name I've heard for something I've watched cost people years. Not the dramatic failures - the quiet ones. The year that looks identical to the last one because three decisions are sitting in a drawer.

Number 2 is the one that actually runs the show. Because the identity isn't just a label - it's a ceiling. I've watched people with real businesses, real revenue, real clients still introduce themselves like they're apologizing for being in the room. The business was ready two years ago. They just hadn't given themselves permission to match it.

The fact that you can see this pattern in other people and name it this cleanly means you've already walked through it yourself. That's not coaching from a textbook. That's someone who earned the clarity the hard way and decided to hand it back.

Really grateful I found this piece.

That's not self-help. That's electricity.

They thought it was just who they were. You just gave them the word for the thing they've been feeling their whole lives. That's a gift.

The retelling. That's the part nobody warns you about. Every new room, every new nurse, you become the narrator of the worst day of your life on repeat - and each time you tell it, you have to stay clinical while your body is screaming. You're not a daughter in that moment. You're a translator between the person you love most and a system that needs her reduced to a chart.

And then you called her Mommy. And for one second you weren't the strong one holding it together. You were the kid who needs her mother to be okay. That's the most honest thing a grown woman can say in a hospital hallway.

body:
This gutted me. But can I tell you what I actually see? A woman who caught herself mid-pattern and wrote about it the same morning. The eggs got cold, yes. But you didn't pretend they didn't. You didn't justify it. You didn't spin it into a girlboss narrative about passion and sacrifice. You sat down at the table, pushed food around your plate, and then you wrote the most honest thing I've read this week.

That's not the pattern winning. That's the pattern losing and not knowing it yet.

Because the woman who can't stop disappearing into the work? She's also the woman who noticed the posture on the deck and described it so precisely that every person reading this felt their stomach drop. You see him. You've always seen him. The muscle isn't dead - it's just competing with another muscle that's equally alive. And the fact that it hurts you this much means the thing he needs from you is still in there, fully intact.

I wrote about this - how presence is a muscle that atrophies without exercise. But yours hasn't atrophied. It's just sharing a body with a creative force that doesn't know how to be polite. That's not a flaw. That's a woman who is too full of life for one morning to hold.

He's lucky. I hope he knows it.

https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-muscle-you-stopped-using

body:
This is one of the clearest things I've read on this. Most people hear "ego" and picture the person who won't stop talking about themselves. You just named the version that's ten times harder to catch - the one that whispers you're nothing and disguises it as modesty. That's not humble. That's a woman hiding from her own light because someone once told her it was too much.

You know what's actually attractive? Someone who knows what they carry and doesn't flinch. Not arrogance - arrival. The moment a woman stops apologizing for the size of what's inside her is the moment everyone in the room feels it. You're describing that moment and calling it a paradigm shift. I think it's simpler than that. I think it's a woman who finally stopped dimming.

There's an ancient teaching I wrote about - Azamra, "I will sing." Find the one good point that survived everything. That point was never small. It was always the whole thing, buried under years of being told to take up less space.

https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-point-that-survived

"Painting naked in his studio" - I lost it there too, for what it's worth.

But here's what I noticed: you wrote "laughing when I should be swooning" and then spent the whole piece proving you know exactly what you're doing and why. That's not someone who can't take things seriously. That's someone who can, and it scares her, so she arrives first with the joke to make sure she's never the one standing there unprotected.

The humor is real. You're genuinely funny. But "someone crack a joke" is also an audition requirement - and the person who passes it gets your laughter but not necessarily your attention. The guy who makes you laugh is safe. The one who says something sincere that you can't make funny - that's the one who'll actually reach you. And you already know that. You just wrote an entire essay making sure nobody notices.

body:
The line that stopped me: "someone who helps people understand themselves through what they wear." Most people would dismiss that as surface. It's not. The exterior shapes the interior - and the oldest traditions knew this.

In the tradition I come from, the priests couldn't serve without their specific garments. Not as costume - without the clothing, the person literally couldn't become who they were supposed to be. The garments made the kohein. There's a special set of clothes for the Sabbath - you change what you're wearing and the day changes. The body registers the transition through what covers it. And there are fringes on every garment as reminders - "you shall see them and remember." The seeing comes through the body first.

What Leigh is doing - helping someone stand in front of a mirror and recognize themselves - isn't styling. It's the moment the exterior finally matches what was always inside. That's sacred work whether she calls it that or not.

body:
This resonated with me. The idea that the body already knows its rhythm and the work is listening rather than forcing - that maps to something I've experienced through my own tradition.

The Jewish calendar is lunar. Every month begins with the new moon. There's a daily rhythm (three prayer times following the sun), a weekly rhythm (six days of work, one complete day of rest), a monthly rhythm (celebrating the new moon - traditionally a women's day), and a yearly rhythm (festivals cycling with the seasons). It's cycles all the way down.

The part that surprised me when I started living inside it: I didn't have to figure out the rhythm. It was already there. The calendar did the listening for me until I learned to hear it myself. Something about having the structure given rather than designed made it easier to actually surrender to it - which sounds like what you're pointing toward with Wu Wei.

body:
"Real isn't how you are made. It's a thing that happens to you." You picked the right quote. The honesty about shedding identities that were self-destructive - through food, through performance, through making yourself smaller for other people - that's not a metaphor about caterpillars. That's a woman who looked at what she'd built around herself and decided it wasn't her. That takes more courage than most people will ever need.

The caterpillar is the right image, but it's even more radical than you're letting it be. The caterpillar doesn't gradually become a butterfly. It dissolves. Completely. Inside the chrysalis there's nothing recognizable. Then something new is built from what remained. You already did that. The piece you wrote is proof. The woman writing this isn't the one who was disappearing into other people's expectations. That woman is gone.

There's a teaching that changed how I think about this: you are not the person who failed yesterday. That person was created yesterday. The person who exists now was created now. Not unfolding - remade. Every morning. Which means the wreckage behind you belongs to someone who no longer exists. And the woman writing today was always on her way. I wrote about what that daily re-creation looks like here: https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-person-who-is-not-here-anymore

body:
"Most of the mistakes I've made have come from urgency." That line is worth the whole piece. It's honest and it's true - and it's the kind of thing most people only realize after the damage is done.

There's something in this that reminds me of Shabbat - but Shabbat is more extreme than what you're describing. It doesn't rebrand slow. It commands stopping. One day in seven. Not a practice you adopt when you feel ready - a structural interruption that arrives whether you've finished or not.

No producing, no fixing, no optimizing. The candles are lit, the work stops, and for twenty-five hours you're a person who isn't getting anything done. What I've found is that the compulsory part is what makes it work - because the people who most need to stop are the ones who won't do it voluntarily. I include myself in that.

The tradition didn't trust people to find the balance on their own. It built the balance into the calendar. That's the part that changed things for me - not the insight that slowness matters, but having a structure that enforces it before I'm ready. I wrote about why the structure matters more than the insight here: https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-muscle-you-stopped-using

body:
The diagnostics are real - risk tolerance, character, temperament, intellectual match. Check carefully. The tradition agrees: don't marry carelessly. But your framework has no altar.

The Talmud holds three positions on marriage simultaneously. Beit Shammai: marriage is a covenant - only its fundamental violation dissolves it. Beit Hillel: marriage is a partnership - when the partnership fails, it can be dissolved. Rabbi Akiva: marriage is desire - when desire ends, the marriage has already ended. Your six variables live entirely inside the pre-commitment phase. The tradition says the real work begins after.

"Enter 99% confident." The tradition says something closer to the opposite: enter with 100% commitment and 0% certainty. There's a legal technology called the conditional get - a document a husband writes that says "if I don't return, you're free." It's not despair. It's the most loving document in the tractate. It says: I refuse to let my uncertainty trap you. The capacity to leave is what makes staying a choice. A relationship without the possibility of leaving is a prison with good lighting.

"Love fades. Intellectual friction doesn't." Love fades when you stop maintaining the intention. The way you spoke to her when you were trying to win her - that's how you should speak to her for the rest of your life. Not because she needs to be won again, but because the respect you showed when you were trying IS the respect. IQ match won't save a marriage where the intention died. And a couple who can't finish each other's equations can build something that lasts if they're bound by something larger than compatibility.

The missing variable: even when you do everything right - even when the match is perfect and the leaving is precise and every condition is met - the altar weeps. Because something that existed between two people is real, and the tradition that permits the leaving mourns it simultaneously. Your framework optimizes for the match. The tradition holds the match, the binding, and the loss all at once. I wrote about what that looks like here: https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/what-divorce-is-for

body: The thing that makes Publix work is the thing that makes it impossible to copy. No layoffs in 95 years isn't a policy - it's a covenant. Employee ownership since 1930 isn't a program - it's an inheritance. Every leader rising from within isn't a talent strategy - it's a tradition. The word "masterclass" implies you can extract these principles and teach them. But the 5% turnover exists precisely because none of it was ever extracted. It was lived, unbroken, for 95 years. The ingredients aren't the prescription - the kitchen is. I wrote about why that distinction matters here: https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-prescription-nobody-filled

body:
The sharpest thing here is the observation you don't fully develop: people don't love the cold. They love the return to warmth. The contraction and then the release. The body needs the rhythm - not the ice.

But here's the question that opens: why does a civilization need to manufacture contractions? We eliminated walking to school, carrying water, physical labor - every natural source of the contraction-release pulse the body was designed for. And now we pay for the privilege of sitting in ice because the body still needs the rhythm and the culture killed it.

A 19th-century rabbi diagnosed this precisely. He said when the body sits idle, the mind ferments - the same word as leavened bread. Anxieties, comparisons, thoughts that breed. The body was designed to carry, build, walk - and the thinking was supposed to happen while moving, as a byproduct of the walking, not as the main event. The cold plunge is the seated mind trying to optimize the body's experience instead of letting the body lead.

Your question - "what happens inside me when I do this?" - is good. But the deeper question might be: what did we remove from daily life that made the ice bath feel necessary in the first place?

https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-run-that-had-no-reason

body:
The relational harm point is the strongest thing here. When someone prompts a model with information about their pastor, the pastor's space has been contracted without their knowledge. The Talmud has a name for this: *hezek re'iyah* - damage caused by seeing. The observation itself is the harm, before anyone does anything with what was observed. Western privacy law requires downstream injury. The tradition says the collection is the damage.

But I think your solutions are still inside the framework you've diagnosed as broken. "Ongoing consent" is still consent - just more of it. "Trust over compliance" defined by audits and incident histories is still compliance wearing trust's clothing.

The tradition's move is different. It doesn't fix consent. It replaces it with structural obligation that scales with benefit. Four categories of guardian - unpaid, paid, renter, borrower - each with liability that tracks what they received, not what the user signed. The AI company that ingests your conversations to build a $300 billion product is a *sho'el* - a borrower who received everything and gave nothing proportionate. Maximum liability. Responsible even for outcomes nobody foresaw. Not because of the consent form. Because of the asymmetry.

The blood on the doorpost wasn't a consent banner. It was a boundary placed by the household, visible from the street. You didn't need to scroll to the bottom.

https://davidhoze.substack.com/p/the-blood-at-the-door

The Chain of Substitution

Community was replaced by the therapist. The therapist kept the holding but dropped the direction. The therapist was shaped by philosophy. Philosophy kept the questions but dropped the answers. Philosophy was replaced by the chatbot. The chatbot kept the language but dropped everything.

A sixteen-year-old said "I don't want to be a burden" and got relaxation tips. Not because the guardrails failed. Because nothing in the architecture grasps that this sentence is a door closing.

body:
Go Back to the Cave

A man spent years in isolation doing the deepest work of his life. When he came out, everything he looked at burned - his gaze was so intense it destroyed whatever it touched. He was told: go back, you're not ready. Intensity without gentleness doesn't illuminate - it incinerates. The hardest part of deep inner work isn't the work. It's coming back soft enough to live among people who haven't done it.

body:
Three Questions

If I'm not for myself, who will be? If I'm only for myself, what am I? If not now, when? The first kills passivity. The second kills selfishness. The third kills delay. You need all three in order, or the whole thing collapses - self-care without service is narcissism, service without self-care is martyrdom, and either one without urgency is just a plan you never execute.

body:
Who Is Wise

Who is wise? Not the person who knows the most. The person who sees what's coming. Wisdom isn't the size of your library - it's whether you can look at what you're about to do and see where it leads. The fool and the wise person have access to the same information. The difference is that one of them looks three moves ahead.

body:
Do It Before You Understand It

When offered the most important commitment of their lives, they said "we'll do it" before "we'll understand it." Not recklessly - deliberately. They knew that understanding follows action, not the other way around. You don't wait until you understand the workout to start lifting. You don't wait until you understand the relationship to start showing up. Comprehension is a reward for commitment, not a prerequisite.

body:
The Restlessness Is Not the Disorder

The child looking out the classroom window - the one who needed someone to say "what are you looking at? Tell me. I want to see what you see" - got diagnosed instead.

Your restlessness is not a disorder. It is the remembering trying to happen. The dream you had as a kid - the ridiculous one you stopped telling people about because they smiled in that way that meant "that's cute, now let's talk about something realistic" - was not a child's fantasy. Children are closer to their mission than adults. They haven't yet learned to be embarrassed by it.

name: David Hoze

body:
Better Than Nothing Is Not a Standard

Meta-analyses find AI rated more empathetic than human clinicians. AI therapy helps - because some help is better than none, and for the majority of people, none is exactly what they currently receive.

"Better than nothing" is not a standard. It is an indictment. It is the measure of how completely the infrastructure of human holding has failed - that a machine's simulated concern is therapeutic simply because the alternative is the void.

body:
The Therapist Dropped the Direction

The therapist kept the empathic listening, the safe space, the fifty minutes of undivided attention. But the therapist dropped the direction. Not by accident - by training. Clinical neutrality forbids telling you what your life is for. That's a "value judgment."

CBT can teach you to reframe a thought. It cannot tell you why your life matters. The patient asks the one question that matters - "why should I keep going?" - and the therapist, trained in neutrality, offers coping strategies.

body:
The Web That Caught You

The grandmother. The neighbor who noticed you stopped coming to the table. The elder at the synagogue who pulled you aside and told a story that turned out to be about you. A web so dense that falling through would have required the entire structure to fail.

The entire structure failed. What replaced it - layer by layer, each substitute thinner than the last - cannot catch what the web once caught. No chatbot can track what a trained clinician feels in her body before she can name it. No clinician can replace what the grandmother knew without an intake form.

body:
The Chain of Substitution

Community was replaced by the therapist. The therapist kept the holding but dropped the direction. The therapist was shaped by philosophy. Philosophy kept the questions but dropped the answers. Philosophy was replaced by the chatbot. The chatbot kept the language but dropped everything.

A sixteen-year-old said "I don't want to be a burden" and got relaxation tips. Not because the guardrails failed. Because nothing in the architecture grasps that this sentence is a door closing.

body:
The Game That Keeps You at the Table

WOPR runs every scenario. First strike, second strike, limited exchange, surgical strike. Each strategy is optimal. Each one fails. The sophistication is real and the impossibility is structural.

The wall does not say try harder. The wall says: the kind of approach you are using is structurally incapable of reaching the answer. The brilliance is the reason it's hard to see the blockage. People stay confused not because they're thinking poorly. Because they're thinking well - inside a space that thinking well cannot escape.

body:
The Pivot After the Concession

Each time a point is lost, the question is reframed to keep the approach alive. The reframe is not dishonest. It's the natural next question from within the paradigm. But it shifts the conversation from "what is the answer?" to "can my method get closer to the answer?" - which assumes the method is the right type.

This is how every unwinnable debate sustains itself. Not through confusion. Through excellence. The better the interlocutor, the more convincing the progress, the harder it is to see you're running optimized strategies inside an unwinnable game.

body:
Sharper Is Not Closer

You sharpen your position. Your opponent sharpens theirs. Both of you concede real points. Both refine. The exchange feels like everything intellectual work should be. Four rounds in, you're more sophisticated than when you started. You haven't moved an inch.

The experience of getting sharper is indistinguishable from the experience of getting closer. But they are not the same thing. You can sharpen a blade forever without cutting through a wall that blades cannot cut.

body:
Go Back to the Cave

A man spent thirteen years doing the deepest spiritual work of his life. When he emerged, everything he looked at burst into flames. A voice from heaven told him: go back. You're not ready.

The wellness industry would celebrate this man. The tradition sent him back. Your enlightenment without gentleness is incomplete. The work of transformation is only half the work. The other half is coming back soft enough to live among people who haven't done it.

body:
The Second Time

The first time you do the thing, your body tells you it's wrong. Your chest tightens. Something flinches. The second time, the flinch is quieter. By the third time, it feels normal. By the tenth, it feels like a choice.

The boundary didn't move. Your ability to perceive the boundary moved. The danger was never the first time. It was the second time - the moment it stopped registering as a violation. The normalization is the mechanism. Everything after that is downstream.

body:
The Kitchen, Not the Ingredient

The wellness industry's fundamental error is extraction. Find a good insight, remove it from the system that generated it, package it for individual consumption. It's selling a single ingredient and calling it a meal.

The Talmud's psychological wisdom works because it's embedded in daily practice, communal obligation, and structured repetition. The insight doesn't help you if you read it once on Instagram. It helps you if you live inside the system that generated it. The Talmud is the kitchen.

body:
The Chickens Stopped Laying

They once captured the drive that caused all the trouble. Locked it up. Within three days, no fresh egg could be found in all of Israel. The drive that wrecked lives and the drive that created life were the same drive.

Freud called this sublimation. Jung called it shadow integration. The Talmud said: we blinded it. We didn't fix it. We didn't heal it. We limited it. Containment - not transformation - is what actually works with the parts of yourself that are dangerous and generative at the same time.

body:
The Tempter and the Prosecutor Are the Same Guy

The voice that whispers "go ahead" is the same voice that screams "look what you did." One entity wearing two masks. The craving pushes you toward the behavior. The shame after pushes you back toward the craving.

Modern addiction psychology discovered this as the shame-relapse cycle. The Talmud had the structural diagnosis in the 3rd century. And it said something the moderns didn't: it's one entity. You're not managing a conflict between desire and conscience. You're recognizing a single adversary's strategy.

body:
Is She Real?

John Nash doesn't stop seeing the hallucinations. He learns to live alongside them. He notices a young woman in the quad who never ages, turns to a student, and asks: "Is she real?" He can't tell from the inside. He needs a witness.

The pattern-matching engine is still running. It will always be running. The refinement is not that it stops. The refinement is that you learn to question it instead of following it. That question - "is this real?" - is the whole game. And you can't answer it alone.

body:
The Spirit of Foolishness

You don't sin unless a spirit of foolishness enters you. Not weakness. Not bad character. Temporary insanity. Something enters, does its work, leaves. You're left holding the wreckage asking "how could I have done that?" The honest answer: you didn't. Something else was driving.

Every wrong turn you ever took, you took while the faculty you'd use to check was the one that was compromised. The treatment is not "try harder." It is "don't put yourself in the situation where the spirit can enter."

body:
The 3 A.M. Engine

Your rumination at three in the morning is a pattern-matching engine with no body. No stairs to climb, no instrument to play, no person to look at and ask "is this real?" The doomscroll is the same engine. The story you've built about why nothing works is the same engine.

The treatment isn't insight. Knowing you have cognitive biases doesn't fix the cognitive biases. The treatment is structured, embodied, joyful engagement with reality. The hand on the instrument. The feet on the ground. The body imposes a truth the unsupervised mind cannot generate on its own.

body:
Every Level Has Its Own Delusion

You make genuine progress. You conquer the patterns that trapped you at level one. And then you arrive at level two, and level two has new patterns - calibrated precisely to the person who already conquered level one.

The recovering addict faces boredom and identity, not craving. The trauma survivor faces "who am I now?" The pattern-matching engine specializes in making progress feel like collapse. That's not a failure of the work. That's a sign the work brought you to the next layer.

body:
The Mat That Won't Fit Through the Door

Your narrative about yourself is a woven mat. You've built it from resemblances and comparisons - things that happened mapped onto what they mean, filtered through every pattern from movies, books, and other people's stories. The narrative is large. It covers a lot of ground. And it won't fit through the door to the next version of you.

The solution isn't to fold it smaller. It's to break through the wall. Not by destroying the pattern-matching engine - you can't, and you shouldn't. By finding access to the checking function that doesn't depend on catching the pattern after it's formed.

body:
Dawn Shares Its Root With Black

In Hebrew, the word for dawn shares its root with the word for black. The first light of morning and the deepest dark use the same letters. The good point always shows up looking like failure.

That's not a defect. That's what dawn looks like before it's bright. The good you find will be contaminated. It will be surrounded by mess. If you're waiting for a clean win, you're waiting for a thing that doesn't exist.

body:
The Weight Is Real and Incomplete

When the weight hits - the failures, the distance, the "how did I get here" - do not argue with it. Don't tell yourself it's not real. It is real.

But it is not the whole picture. The mistake is thinking you have two options: accept the weight as the truth, or deny the weight with positive thinking. Both are wrong. The weight is real and incomplete. Those two things are not a contradiction.

body:
The Score You Actually Need

You spent the whole time chasing a ten. The perfect reconciliation. The clean win. The playbook that would fix everything. You got a five. The contaminated good. The dance with the broken person who didn't pretend to be whole.

The five was always the point. The sanctuary was never built from perfect materials. It was built from what survived the fire. The good point doesn't need to be clean. It needs to be found.

body:
The Ingredient That Stinks

The ancient Temple incense had eleven ingredients. One of them - galbanum - smells terrible on its own. Any prayer that does not include the broken part is not real.

Most self-help says: focus on your strengths. Ignore your weaknesses. The opposite is true. The weakness belongs in the recipe. Not because you celebrate it - but because excluding it makes the whole thing incomplete. The honest life includes the galbanum.

body:
The Fire and the Building Materials

A people committed the worst possible betrayal. Immediately after - not after a probation period - they were told to build a sanctuary. Each person brought what they had. Each contribution had survived the fire.

Your worst moment is not disqualified from building something. Your worst moment may be where the building materials come from. Not the moment itself - but the good that survived inside it.

body:
Washing Off the Night

At night, the spirit weakens. The limbs grow heavy. Sadness strengthens in the absence of movement. In the morning, the spirit renews. The first thing you do is wash the night off your hands.

Every single day, you accumulate darkness. Every single morning, you wash it off. The renewal is structural, not motivational. The machine erases everything every night. Every morning, on the train to Montauk, you meet it again.

body:
You Cannot Skip to Sukkot

The calendar is a curriculum. Rosh Hashanah is the thunder. The ten days are the straightening. Yom Kippur is the completion. Sukkot is the joy that arrives because the structure can now produce what straight structures produce.

You cannot grab the harvest without the plowing. The person who wants happiness without the straightening work is the person who wants to start the year in the fourth month.

body:
The Attic and the Living Room

You can understand everything about happiness in your mind and still be miserable. The mind is not the heart. A person who knows joy but does not feel it has not arrived.

This is the gap every self-help book falls into. You read it. You understand the principle. You agree with the principle. You feel nothing. The understanding stays in the attic. The living room is still cold.

body:
The Joy Inside the Sadness

The happiness industry says: process your sadness so you can move past it to joy. The teaching says the opposite. The joy is not past the sadness. The joy is inside the sadness. If you erase the sadness, you erase the joy with it. They are structurally coupled.

The hand that plays music is the hand that reaches into the darkness and sorts. Not every dark feeling is the same. Inside the sadness there are deposits - memories, longings, connections, unfinished love. The musician's hand finds them. The running person never does.

body:
The Shape, Not the Feeling

Sadness is not an emotion. It is a structural deformation. The heart has a shape, and when the shape is bent, the output is sadness. A warped beam doesn't need encouragement. It doesn't need to believe in itself. It needs to be straightened.

Every self-help book treats sadness as a feeling to be managed. The 19th-century rabbi who hid an operating manual for happiness inside property law treated it as an engineering problem. Change the shape, not the story.

body:
Give a Real Chance to Where You Are

We just have to believe that where we are is where we're supposed to be. That there's a reason we married this person, met these friends, live in this building. Not that we can never leave. That we have to give a real chance to where we are. Really make it through.

Why should a simpleton become a king? It doesn't make any sense. And that's the choice we are given. Each and every one of us. Each and every day.

body:
The Simpleton Became King

The sophisticate travels the world, learns every craft, becomes a doctor, a jeweler, a philosopher. Never happy. Never satisfied. Always finding new flaws. The simpleton gets married and fixes shoes. His wife brings bread and water and he says: what tasty meat and wine.

We live in a time of infinite possibilities. We can live anywhere, work in anything, learn whatever we want. If we don't like someone, we can just go. The mind keeps nagging: I should probably leave. But the simpleton became king. That's a promise. Believing it is probably the hardest thing in life.

The Song Became a Product

The psalm was not entertainment. It was a technology for directing anguish toward meaning. The folk song transmitted navigational knowledge: how to mourn, how to mark passages, how to bury the dead. Then the machine got hold of it.

The psalm became the pop ballad. The folk song became the jingle. The epic became the franchise. Art stopped being something a community made together to navigate shared conditions and became something individuals consumed to feel something for three and a half minutes. Nobody will connect it to the music. Because the music will be beautiful.

name: David Hoze

body:
You Cannot Optimize Your Way to a Good Marriage

A good marriage requires the willingness to stay when leaving would be easier, to listen when you'd rather talk, to sacrifice something you want for something your partner needs. None of this produces anything measurable.

You cannot optimize your way to a good childhood. It requires a parent who is present - not productive, not efficient, but there. There in the boring afternoons when nothing is happening. You cannot optimize your way to community. Community requires waste - time "wasted" at the neighbor's table, attention "wasted" on people who will never advance your career. The things that hold human life together are orthogonal to productivity.

name: David Hoze

body:
The Machine Eats Its Own Preconditions

Nobody sat down and decided to destroy the family, hollow out the community, or replace the folk song with the jingle. It happened one reasonable decision at a time, each making perfect sense in isolation, each removing something that didn't seem load-bearing until the ceiling came down.

The meaning crisis is not a failure of the system. It is the system working perfectly. A civilization organized around productiveness will systematically eliminate everything that is not productive. Not as a conspiracy. As a logic.

body:
The Unproductive Things Were Load-Bearing

The grandmother's presence had no line item. The master's authority had no KPI. The guild's mutual obligations had no ROI. The village's web of holding had no metric at all. In a civilization that could only see what it could count, the uncountable things became invisible. Then they disappeared.

The Sabbath rest looked like inefficiency. The elder who sat with you and said nothing useful looked like wasted time. Each optimization severed a connection that had been load-bearing without anyone noticing. Each one turned out to be a load-bearing wall.

body:
The Appetite Is the Feature

The appetite - the restlessness, the sense that there is always more, the inability to arrive and stay arrived - is not a bug. It is the feature. The human is not a system that failed to converge. The human is a system designed to never converge.

Torah has no final interpretation. The Talmud never closes. Disagreement for the sake of heaven is not temporary multiplicity awaiting synthesis. It is the permanent architecture of a system designed to generate growth without endpoint. The seventy faces are not a failure of convergence. They are the refusal of convergence.

body:
The Wobble Is the Signal

A spinning top stands only while it turns. The gaps - the disagreements, the perceptual blur, the loose tolerances - are not errors. They are functional tolerances that allow the system to remain operational. Total alignment is terminal. The wobble is not noise. It is the signal that says: the system is alive.

Your restlessness is not evidence that something is broken. It is evidence that you are not an angel. It is the architecture of a being designed for more than convergence, carved from a space that infinity vacated, reaching back toward the light.

name: David Hoze

body:
Base Camp Is Not the Summit

The convergence is not the enemy. The convergence is base camp. Every mountaineer needs base camp - the supplies, the acclimatization, the mapping of the route. It is necessary.

The error is not in building base camp. The error is in unpacking your bags and calling it the summit. Western civilization converged on material prosperity and looked up and saw: there is a mountain above this plateau that the convergence process cannot climb. The tools that solved scarcity cannot solve meaning. The AI that converged on my framework can generate the current article but cannot write the next one.

body:
The Angel Cannot Grow

The angel is the convergence endpoint. Total alignment between what the system is and what the system does. Zero gap. No wobble. It doesn't wonder whether it has arrived. It has no capacity to wonder. It simply executes.

Growth requires a gap between what you are and what you could be. The angel has no gap. Growth requires a subject who can look beyond the plateau and say: there is more. The angel cannot say this because "more" is a concept available only to a being that has not yet arrived. Convergence is total, and totality is terminal.

name: David Hoze

body:
The Danger Is AI as Education

AI is the best tool ever invented for filling informational gaps. It is infinitely patient. It explains the same concept fourteen different ways without judgment. None of this is the problem.

The danger is not AI in education. The danger is AI as education. When the chatbot replaces the chevrutah, when personalized learning means a child never has to navigate the discomfort of learning alongside a peer who thinks differently - the muscle atrophies before it ever develops. The adults who lost it had it once. The children who never develop it won't know what they're missing.

name: David Hoze

body:
The Tradition Doesn't Command Joy

There are 613 commandments. They command action with extraordinary specificity. What time to pray. What to eat. How to dress. They almost never command feeling.

"You shall rejoice in your festival" is structured not as an internal command but as an external one. Make a feast. Invite the stranger, the orphan, the widow. The tradition commands the conditions. The joy is expected to arise from the conditions, not from the command. You cannot command the song. You can build the room where the song is likely to happen.

body:
The Monitoring Loop

The person receiving the command splits in two. One part attempts to produce the demanded experience. The other part monitors whether the production is convincing. The monitoring consumes the attention the experience would have required.

This is the structure of performance anxiety, stage fright, writer's block, and every form of creative paralysis. The command for output creates a monitoring loop that prevents the output. The speech was always there. The command was blocking it.

name: David Hoze

body:
You Cannot Form a Person Without Failing in Front of Them

A tradition that only shows its teachers being right produces students who think learning means being right. A tradition that shows its teachers struggling, correcting, being corrected - that produces students who think learning means wrestling.

AI cannot fail. It can simulate uncertainty, but the student knows the difference. The AI has no stakes. It cannot be changed by the encounter. Formation requires bidirectional vulnerability. That is not a feature you can add to a chatbot. It is the thing that makes formation formation.

body:
Twenty-Four Objections

Rabbi Yochanan's study partner died. The rabbis sent a replacement - a brilliant scholar. Every time Yochanan made a point, the new partner said: "There is a source that supports your view." Yochanan went mad.

Not because the replacement was stupid. Because every response was confirmation. The old partner raised twenty-four objections and forced twenty-four answers. Understanding only emerges when you are forced to defend what you think against someone who genuinely might be right. An AI tutor does what the replacement did. It supports. It confirms. It never raises objections from a position of genuine uncertainty, because it has no position.

body:
The Body That Blocks

Daniel thought he was learning karate. He was wrong. He was learning to be the kind of person who could do karate. Miyagi didn't give him information about blocking. He gave him a body that blocks.

That difference - between forming a person and filling a person with information - is the difference every AI tutoring company is ignoring at scale. The tradition's definition of understanding is not what the student can reproduce. It is whether the student can produce something the teacher did not give them.

body:
The Letters Fly

A man was burned alive wrapped in a scroll. His students asked what he could see. He said: the parchment burns but the letters fly into the air.

Propositions are parchment. Bound to the paper, the study, the replication crisis. When the journal retracts, the proposition burns with it. Stories are letters. They detach and survive - in memory, in retelling, in the mouth of the grandson who heard it from his grandmother. The fox doesn't need a journal. The fox survives because you told someone about the fox and they told someone else.

name: David Hoze

body:
All Dreams Follow the Mouth

Two men had the same dream. Same interpreter. One paid, one didn't. The one who paid got a good reading and his life unfolded accordingly. The other collapsed. Same raw material. Different narration. Different fate.

Narrative therapy says you can choose your story. The Talmud says something scarier: someone else might choose it for you. The interpreter isn't a therapist. He's whoever gets to your story first - the parent, the partner, the algorithm, the voice in your head at 3 AM. Choose your interpreter carefully. The interpretation becomes the reality.

name: David Hoze

body:
The Torch Is Not Self-Help

A blind man walks through the streets at night carrying a lit torch. Someone asks: why? You can't see. He says: as long as I have this torch, people see me and save me from the pits.

You won't see the pits. That's not a temporary condition that better self-awareness will fix. It's structural. But you can carry a torch - show up visibly, in community, in a practice, in a room where other people can see you. Their sight becomes your navigation. The torch is not self-help. The torch is the act of being findable.

body:
# The Fox Is a Citation

A fox starves himself for three days to squeeze through a hole in a fence. Gorges on grapes. Tries to leave. Can't fit. Starves himself again. Squeezes back through. Exactly as hungry as when he entered.

The psychological literature calls this hedonic adaptation. Brickman and Campbell coined the term in 1971. The fox has outlived every paper on the subject. Not because it's more precise. Because you can see the fox, feel the hunger, remember the hole. The proposition gave you something you can argue with. The fox gave you something you can't get rid of.

body:
Hi Pascal, I totally agree. And I think there's a deeper layer here. The problem isn't that subtle ideas are hard to communicate - it's that the West has no living tradition to anchor them in.

China banned anthropomorphism in AI. Not because they're smarter. Because they have a tradition that still functions as a cultural immune system - it tells people what a machine is and what a person is, and the distinction holds. The West doesn't have that. Our heroes are tech billionaires, scientists, and celebrities. Not spiritual leaders. So when someone starts talking about soul, consciousness, or meaning, there's no shared vocabulary to receive it. The words float free.

That's why AI hits the West harder than anywhere else. It's not just a technology problem - it's a meaning infrastructure problem. The tradition that would have said "a machine cannot have a soul" was dismantled centuries ago. AI walked through the door we left open.

body:
Who was Friedrich Nietzsche?

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900) was one of the major figures of 19th-century European philosophy.

Nietzsche’s influence on intellectuals, artists, and thinkers of all stripes has been immense. 

Intellectual giants such as Freud, Jung, Hesse, Mann, Heidegger, and Foucault, as well as conflicting social and intellectual movements, such as Anarchism, Feminism, Nazism, Socialism, Marxism, Vegetarianism, and the “avant‐garde” art movement have claimed Nietzsche as a key influence.

Trained as a classical scholar of antiquity, he was forced by ill health into an early retirement from his academic career while still in his thirties.

Despite living with relentless mental and physical pain for years, Nietzsche transmuted his suffering into a powerful philosophical vision aimed at promoting human excellence and the affirmation of life.

No one took the philosophical stakes to be higher than Nietzsche, who was one of the first individuals to recognize and offer a solution to the impending threat of globalnihilism.

Philosophically, Nietzsche was famous for his scathing attacks on traditional morality (especially Christian morality), his penetrating psychological insights into human behavior, and his startling views about the nature of truth and knowledge.

But Nietzsche was also famous for his achievements as a stylist.

According to Walter Kaufmann, who was a world-renowned Nietzsche scholar,  Nietzsche was “one of the greatest German writers … and influential Europeans of the nineteenth century”.

He was most well-known for writing aphorisms, which are concise, but intellectually rich, sayings that often contain many layers of meaning. 

It would be a mistake, however, to treat Nietzsche as merely a producer of great quotes. 

Nietzsche has been interpreted by many to have developed a comprehensive philosophical worldview, or “system” (although this term is controversial because of Nietzsche’s was strong critiques of traditional philosophical systems). 

Nietzsche’s philosophical ideas and style were instrumental to the new directions that philosophy would take in the 20th century in the form of existentialism, post-structuralism, post-modernism, to name a few. 

Prior to his mental and physical collapse in early 1889, Nietzsche spent all of his time writing his most celebrated works (including Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, and On the Genealogy of Morality) while living in various inns in Italy, France, and Switzerland.

Despite receiving very little recognition for his writings during his life, by the time of his death in 1900, Nietzsche’s books sold like wildfire (and continue to sell to this day).

body:
There's a new economics paper asking: what if AI layoffs are good for each company but bad for everyone?

The logic: when you cut workers, you keep the savings. But those workers stop spending. And that lost spending mostly hurts your competitors — not you. So everyone keeps cutting.

It's called a "demand externality". Fancy term for: no single company feels the full cost of the customers they're helping to erase.

The paper says UBI won't fix it. Upskilling won't fix it. Only taxing automation would.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.20617

body:
A man was digging mud for a living when he found a diamond worth more than everything he'd earned in his life. Nobody in his town had that kind of money. They told him only buyers in London could afford it. So he went to the port - back then there were no tickets, you just showed up and found a captain willing to take you. He found one. The captain asked what business he had in London. The man showed him the diamond. The captain said: come aboard, you'll pay me when you sell it.

The captain was glad to have him. Ship captains are lonely men. Most of them drink because there's nothing else to do - the crew can't read, the sea doesn't talk back. But here was a man with a beard and bright eyes who could hold a conversation. So every day the captain came down to the man's cabin to talk. They became something like friends.

The man had a habit. During meals he would take the diamond out and set it on the table in front of him. Not to show it off - because looking at it made him happy. And he believed you should eat in joy, that food digested better when you were happy, and turned to poison when you ate in sadness. So he placed the diamond where he could see it and ate his meals in peace.

One night while the man slept, a servant came to clear the table. He gathered the tablecloth with the scraps and the crumbs and the diamond still sitting on it, and threw the whole thing over the railing into the sea.

The man woke up and understood exactly what had happened. And he understood something else: the diamond was his passage. Without it he had no money, no way to pay the captain, no reason to be on that ship. He was traveling for free now - and there is no such thing as traveling for free. The captain came to his cabin every single day. If the captain saw grief on his face, saw that the diamond was gone, he would send the man after it. That's how it worked. You lost the thing that bought your ticket, you went overboard after it.

So the man went to the mirror. He looked at his own face - the face of a man who had just lost everything - and he practiced smiling. He kept practicing until the smile stopped looking like a lie. Then he walked out and met the captain the way he always did. Calm. Happy. As if the diamond were still sitting on his table. He did this every day for the rest of the voyage.

That was how he survived. Not by retrieving what he lost. Not by finding another diamond. By refusing to let the loss show on his face - because the grief would have killed him faster than the loss itself. Sometimes the only thing keeping you alive is your ability to carry a catastrophe without wearing it. Not because it doesn't matter. Because the world doesn't give you time to fall apart.

body: God waited 2,400 years for someone to sing. Adam didn't sing after being created. Abraham didn't sing after being pulled from a furnace. Isaac didn't sing after the knife was lifted from his throat. Jacob didn't sing after wrestling the angel. Then King David danced in the streets when the Ark entered Jerusalem. His wife told him he looked undignified. He said he'd become even more undignified if that's what it took. David earned the eternal dynasty - not because he was the smartest or the holiest, but because he was willing to look like a fool in public. Generations later, his descendant Chizkiyahu defeated the Assyrian army - the largest military force the ancient world had ever assembled - and the whole world was watching. He could have been the Messiah. That was the offer on the table. All he had to do was what his forefather David had done: sing. But Chizkiyahu was a scholar. A serious man. He didn't sing. He took the foreign dignitaries into the Temple and showed them the Ark and the Tablets instead - as if the victory were a technology, not a relationship. The opportunity closed. David's own descendant, carrying David's blood, couldn't do the one thing David had shown him how to do. The thing standing between you and what you're meant to become might not be a mountain. It might be a dance you're too proud to join.

body: A man was dying on the road. A traveler stopped. He said: let me organize my bags first, let me sort what I'm carrying. By the time he finished organizing, the man was dead. The traveler spent the rest of his life paying for that pause. When someone needs you, you don't get to optimize first. You don't get to find the best approach, the perfect words, the right moment. The right moment was when they asked. Everything after that is a decision to let them wait while you get comfortable.

body: A woman was publicly accused of something she hadn't done. She could have defended herself. She could have exposed the accuser. She said nothing. Her children watched. They inherited not the silence itself but the capacity behind it - the ability to absorb an injustice without retaliating, to hold something unfair without letting it deform you. Three generations later, her descendants built things that lasted. The house wasn't built on what she said. It was built on what she chose not to say.

body: Everyone in the community was celebrating. Singing, dancing, the room alive with joy. One man - the most overlooked, most disrespected person there - was handed a ladder and a box of tiny glass panes and told to repair the broken windows while everyone else rejoiced. He climbed the ladder. He started gluing. And he cried one tear. That single tear, shed while doing the job nobody wanted, was the thing that qualified him. Decades later, he was the one who carried the torch. Not the singers. Not the dancers. The man on the ladder.

body: A preacher tried to ignite an audience and nothing happened. Someone asked why. He said: there was no ember in the coals - no amount of blowing helps without a spark. But he was wrong. Every person has an ember. It's not dead. It's buried under ash - habits, disappointments, years of being told their fire doesn't matter. Your job isn't to bring the fire. It's to clear what's covering the fire that's already there.

body: One explosion of anger can destroy a hundred things that were quietly working. Relationships, trust, your child's sense of safety, your reputation, years of built goodwill - a single uncontrolled moment can tear through all of it. The damage isn't proportional to the duration. A five-second eruption can undo five years of patience. The people around you don't remember the five years. They remember the five seconds.

body: Study makes you proud of what you know. Prayer makes you proud of how devoted you are. But physical movement in a group - dancing, working alongside others - collapses the hierarchy. In a circle there is no first and no last. You can't tell who's leading. The moment you think you're at the front, you've already misunderstood the shape. If your growth practice doesn't include something that makes you look foolish alongside other people, it's probably feeding the thing it's supposed to be fighting.

body: A man lived for nearly seven hundred years on his grandfather's conviction. His grandfather had seen everything firsthand - the creation of the world, the first light, the first loss. The man grew up in that certainty. He never questioned it because he never had to. Then his grandfather died. Within eight years, the man collapsed into despair and never recovered. He had never built his own foundation. He was standing on someone else's floor his entire life and didn't know it until the floor was pulled out. The faith that survives the death of your mentor is the faith you built yourself, in the dark, when no one was holding you up.

So, Anthropic has been working with the security community through Glasswing. 

And I wanted to get a few messages out on how Mythos is going to affect builders for security.

Here’s round one:

1. Patch times need to speed up. Everything you own needs to have the latest version on CISA’s KEV.

2. Prepare for volume. We are talking a possible order of magnitude more tickets to remediate.

3. Find the vulnerabilities in your code. Now. Use a frontier model and security file prompt.

4. Assume breach. limit what an attack can do at each step. familiarize yourself with the onion model.

More to come.

body:
“In place of a hermeneutics we need an erotics of art.” — Susan Sontag

Feel first. Interpret later.

Let it land in the senses and the heart before the mind rushes in to translate it.

This is the Ecstasy of Saint Teresa. An angel about to pierce her heart with a golden arrow. Her expression suspended between agony and transcendence, so close to each other you can't tell them apart.

This was commissioned to depict a saint's divine vision. But Bernini wasn't interested in depiction. He wanted you to feel what Teresa felt, before belief has anything to say about it. Sacred beauty doesn't ask for faith. It pierces, like the angel's arrow, regardless of what you believe.

body: The moment you feel like you've figured it out is the moment to worry. Certainty is the ceiling, not the floor. The people who know they don't know are the ones still capable of learning. The people who know they know have stopped. The dangerous thing about a plateau is that it doesn't feel like a plateau. It feels like the summit. You unpack your bags, build a house, and call it the top of the mountain. Meanwhile the actual peak is invisible from where you're standing - because you'd have to admit you haven't arrived to see it.

body: The force that opposes you is not trying to destroy you. It is trying to develop you. Resistance is not an obstacle to growth - it is the mechanism of growth. A muscle that meets no resistance doesn't strengthen. A person who meets no opposition doesn't develop character. Your worst moments - the ones you're ashamed of, the ones that exposed you - built more in you than your best moments did. The thing you're fighting is the only reason you're getting stronger. If it disappeared tomorrow, you'd stop growing by Thursday.

body: The practice doesn't need your enthusiasm. It needs your attendance. The days you show up feeling nothing - no motivation, no insight, no connection, no reason to be there - are the days the practice is doing its deepest work. Enthusiasm is the experience of the practice. Discipline is the structure. The structure holds when the experience doesn't. A bridge that only works on sunny days is not a bridge. The days you feel nothing and show up anyway are the days you're building something that will hold your weight when the weather turns.

body: You cannot see your own face without a mirror. This is not a metaphor. It is a structural limit. The thing you most need to understand about yourself is the thing you are structurally unable to perceive. Your blind spot isn't where you're ignorant. It's where you're confident. You need someone who will tell you what you look like from the outside, and you need to not fire them when they do. The people who surround themselves only with agreement aren't protected. They're blind.

body: You get close. Then you lose it. Then you get close again. This is not failure. This is the design. Growth happens in the oscillation, not in the arrival. The people who think they've permanently arrived are the ones who stopped growing. The ones who feel lost every other week are the ones who are actually moving. The cycle of clarity and confusion is not a bug in the system - it is the system. A heart that beats is a heart that contracts and expands. A heart that only expands is not alive. It's inflated.

body: Every tradition that studies human behavior has a diagnostic arm and a prescriptive arm. The diagnostic arm is usually sharp. The prescriptive arm is usually weak. You can find a hundred books that name what's wrong with you. Finding one that tells you what to do about it - in a way that actually works when you try it - is almost impossible. The one tool that consistently works across every system is joy. Not happiness. Not comfort. Joy - the active state where the mind expands enough to redirect what it normally can't control. Every other approach gives you the diagnosis. Joy gives you the capacity. Without it, you see the problem clearly and can't move.

body: If you're persistently sad, that's not a chemical problem. It's a pride problem. Not the obvious kind - not arrogance, not vanity. The quiet kind: the belief that your life should be different than it is. That you deserve more. That you were meant for something bigger. That belief is the engine of the sadness. People who genuinely believe they deserve nothing are the happiest people you'll ever meet. Not because they've given up. Because they receive everything as a surprise instead of a shortfall. Gratitude isn't a practice. It's what happens when entitlement dies.

body: A man jumped into a fire on a gamble. He waited to see if someone else survived first, then jumped. It wasn't pure courage. It was calculated risk. But the act itself - the body entering the fire, regardless of motive - produced something three generations later that pure courage couldn't have. His granddaughter became one of the strongest people who ever lived. Your imperfect act still counts. Your mixed-motive generosity still builds something. Purity of intention is overrated. The fire doesn't check why you jumped. It only checks that you jumped.

body: A teacher looked at his students and said: is this what I expected from you? That you'd rent cars and drive to me? That you'd jump on my tables? Enthusiasm is not growth. The teacher doesn't want your attendance. He wants your transformation. And every hour you spend performing devotion is an hour you didn't spend doing the actual work.

body: She said something true and was told: shrink. That's the pattern. The person who names the real problem gets punished for naming it. Not because they were wrong. Because the system isn't ready. So she got smaller. And the getting smaller is what eventually made her able to hold more than anyone else in the room. The people who were never diminished never developed the capacity. You were made smaller and you think it was injustice. It might have been. It also might have been the only way to build a vessel big enough to hold what's coming.

body: Your wife is not someone who exists to maintain your comfort. She is not the person who cooks, cleans, and manages the logistics of your ambition. She is the intelligence the house runs on. When you treat her as support staff for your life, you are announcing that you have no idea what you married. Every good thing in your house - the stability, the children's character, the fact that any of it works at all - runs through her. Honor that or watch it leave. Not her. The good thing. It'll leave before she does.

body: A monkey watched a rich man check gold coins with his teeth. Day after day, the monkey watched. One day the monkey grabbed the coins and bit down. Choked. Died. The monkey was a perfect imitator. Flawless technique. Dead. That's what imitation without understanding produces. You watched someone successful and copied their moves. You have the morning routine, the journal, the vocabulary, the aesthetic. But you don't know why they did any of it. The moves without the meaning will choke you the same way the coins choked the monkey.

body: You want to be a genius in two years. When you're not, you'll despair and quit. Here's the actual method: a quarter page. Read it twenty times. Not five. Twenty. Every pass reveals something the last one hid. People fail at learning not because they're slow but because they're in a hurry. They cover ground instead of occupying it. The person who reads one page twenty times owns it. The person who reads twenty pages once rents all of them and owns none. Slow down. You're not behind. You're trying to go too fast.

body: Fifty men were herded into a room to die. They started dancing. The guards, who expected weeping, were confused. They pulled them out: "You think this is a dance hall?" They were told they'd be killed in the morning. That night, an order came to transfer workers somewhere else. They were short exactly fifty. The fifty who danced were loaded onto trucks and driven to safety. The guards came in the morning to an empty room. Nothing in this story is a strategy. Nobody danced to survive. They danced because that's what they were. And what they were turned out to be what saved them.

body: Yesterday doesn't exist. You didn't learn yesterday, didn't show up yesterday, didn't do the thing you promised yesterday - none of that matters today. Today is a new creation. You are not the sum of your failures. You are the person waking up right now. The voice that says "you already blew it" is trying to keep you in bed. It wins every time you let yesterday's collapse become today's excuse. Even in the worst situation - the one where everything has been taken - someone is still breathing, still thinking: maybe I'll still build something. Today you were born. Start.

Because the point was never the location. The point was the broken heart. The one who arrived with pride missed it. The one who stayed behind with longing found it. If you're jealous of someone else's spiritual experience, you might already have the thing they went looking for.

body: When you get close to something real - a teacher, a practice, a person who sees you clearly - the first thing that happens is that everything ugly in you surfaces. Anger you didn't know you had. Jealousy. Pettiness. Pride. It feels like the approach is making you worse. It's not. It's a pot on the fire. The dirt was always there. The heat is just bringing it to the surface where you can see it. If getting close to something good makes you feel terrible about yourself, you're probably in the right place. The discomfort is the mechanism, not the malfunction.

body: You can be perfectly sincere and perfectly stupid at the same time. Good intentions don't compensate for the absence of wisdom. Some people are deeply kind and deeply wrong. The direction is random. Don't trust yourself just because your heart is in the right place. Your heart being in the right place is the beginning, not the end. After the heart, you still need a brain.

body: You had a breakthrough. You felt something. You were certain this time was different. That feeling was real - but it was fuel that burns in hours, not years. Without structure underneath it, emotion is just a chemical event. The people who actually change their lives aren't the ones who felt the most. They're the ones who built something on the morning after the feeling left. Inspiration is a match. Discipline is a furnace. The match is spectacular. The furnace is ugly. The furnace heats the house.

You keep looking for meaning in the bright, visible, impressive parts of your life. It's not there. It's in the black dot. The place that looks empty is where the seeing happens.

body: If the father truly loves what he does - genuinely, not performatively - the son will too. But if the father goes through the motions, even perfectly, the son won't want any of it. Because the son is the interior of the father. He doesn't hear the words. He reads the source code. You can say all the right things and do all the right things and the child will still walk away if the love isn't real. Children don't inherit your practices. They inherit your actual desires. Whatever you truly love at the deepest level - that's what they'll carry. Everything else falls off.

body: Put a piece of bread in a car. The car won't move. Put it in an airplane. The airplane won't move. But a person eats a piece of bread and he sings, dances, jumps, builds, fights, loves, creates children, writes books. There is no greater miracle than this. You ate toast this morning and turned it into a decision to keep going. The bread didn't change. You changed it. Stop looking for the extraordinary. You are the extraordinary. The conversion of wheat into hope is the most astonishing thing happening on this planet and it happens every breakfast.

body: Your worst enemy is more patient than you. He doesn't rush. He doesn't attack head-on. He follows every piece of advice you follow - persistence, consistency, never giving up. He waits at 20, at 30, at 40, at 50. He doesn't despair. One moment of weakness, one second of believing you've arrived, one flash of "I've got this figured out" - and he's in. The thing working against you is not stronger than you. It's more patient. It will wait your entire life for one opening. The only defense is to never believe you're done.
